content.content:
1	# Audio
2	
3	Frame Job mixes sound from every clip that has it: a camera clip, an audio-only file, a microphone recording or a nest. Each clip has its own level, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan and mono fold, and each track can be muted or soloed. Two commands do the measuring for you. Normalize sets a clip's level from its loudest moment, and Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by their sound. The preview and the export use the same mix, so what you hear while editing is what gets written.
4	
5	## Where audio lives
6	
7	There is only one kind of track. Any track can hold a clip with sound, whether it is a video file, an audio-only file (a voice-over, music, a recorder's take) or a clip you split off with Detach Audio. A clip with sound shows its waveform in the timeline.
8	
9	The waveform shows the level of the file itself, so moving the Volume slider doesn't redraw it. It's drawn faded when the clip is muted, when its track is muted, or when another track's solo silences it. A track that holds only sound clips is drawn as a shorter lane than a track with pictures.
10	
11	When the selection includes at least one clip that plays sound, the Clip tab of the inspector shows a **Sound** sub-tab. A clip counts as having sound when its file has an audio track and its audio is switched on, or when it is a nest that holds audio. The Sound sub-tab has six sections, in this order:
12	
13	1. **Volume**: level, gain read-out, Mute and Normalize
14	2. **Fades**: fade in and fade out
15	3. **Ducking**: lowers every other clip while this one plays
16	4. **Noise Reduction**
17	5. **Compressor**
18	6. **Mix**: pan, mix to mono and Detach Audio
19	
20	Noise Reduction, Compressor and Mix appear in the order the sound passes through them. Volume, the fades and ducking are applied last, like a fader.
21	
22	Every section header has a summary and a Reset button that appears when the section differs from its default. The summaries read:
23	
24	| Section | Summary |
25	|---|---|
26	| Volume | "muted", "silent" (at 0 %), or the gain, for example "+3.5 dB" |
27	| Fades | both lengths, for example "0.50 · 1.00 s", or "none" |
28	| Ducking | the duck level, for example "20%", or "off" |
29	| Noise Reduction | the amount, for example "50%", or "off" |
30	| Compressor | the ratio, for example "3.0:1", or "off" |
31	| Mix | "centre", "mono", or the pan position, for example "left 40" |
32	
33	 When you change a control with several clips selected, the change goes to all of them. A control whose clips hold different values is marked mixed.
34	
35	### Sound on a nest
36	
37	A nest clip has the same Sound sub-tab, but not every control reaches the clips inside it:
38	
39	- **Volume, Mute and the fades** on a nest clip scale everything inside it. Turning a nest down turns all of it down, and muting it silences all of it.
40	- **Mix to mono** on a nest clip folds the nest's whole mix.
41	- **Ducking** on a nest clip lowers the rest of the project for the nest's whole length.
42	- **Pan, the compressor and noise reduction** set on a nest clip have no effect. Open the nest (⌘↓) and set them on the clips inside.
43	
44	*Agents:* `set_audio` (`clips`, `patch`) changes any of these properties on one or more clips. Its patch keys are `volume`, `muted`, `fade_in`, `fade_out`, `duck`, `mono`, `keep_pitch`, `pan`, `compressor` and `noise_reduction`. Setting `duck` or `compressor` to null turns it off. `get_project` reads them back.
45	
46	## Volume
47	
48	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
49	|---|---|---|---|
50	| Volume | The clip's level as a percentage. The slider covers 0–400 %; type a higher value in the field, up to 3200 %. Above 400 % the slider's knob stays at the right end. Quick picks: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 400. | 0–3200 % | 100 % |
51	| Gain | Read-only: the volume in dB (for example "+6.0 dB"), or "silent" at 0 %. | — | +0.0 dB |
52	| Mute | Silences the clip without changing its volume. | on / off | off |
53	| Normalize | Sets the volume from the clip's own loudest moment (see below). | — | — |
54	
55	The section's summary reads "muted", "silent" or the gain in dB. Reset puts the volume back to 100 % and turns Mute off.
56	
57	You can animate volume, Mute and the fades with actions. While an action is selected, the Volume row, the Mute checkbox and the Fade in and Fade out rows write that action's end state, so a level moves across the action's span. Pan, Mix to mono, Keep pitch, the compressor, noise reduction and ducking can't be animated. They always change the clip's own settings, even with an action selected.
58	
59	### Normalize
60	
61	**Normalize** sets each selected clip's volume so that its loudest moment reaches **−1 dBFS**. It's the button in the Volume section, and it's also **Clip ▸ Normalize**.
62	
63	- **It measures the material, not the mix.** The level is read from the clip's cached waveform over the part of the file that actually plays. The clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo don't affect the reading.
64	- **It replaces the volume** rather than multiplying it, so pressing it a second time changes nothing (the second press beeps).
65	- **Each clip gets its own gain.** Normalize doesn't match levels across a selection. However many clips are selected, it is one undo step, named "Normalize".
66	- **It writes the clip's base level**, even when the playhead is inside an action. With an action selected, the button carries a small boxed "clip" tag to show this.
67	- **It leaves Mute alone.**
68	- **It can go past 400 %.** A quiet recording, such as a desktop USB microphone's, is turned up as far as it needs, up to the 3200 % ceiling (about +30 dB). Only a clip whose peak is quieter than about −31 dBFS can't reach −1 dBFS. It is turned up to 3200 % and stops there.
69	
70	Some clips in a selection are skipped and the rest are still normalized: nests (their level lives in the clips inside them), shapes, titles and silent movies. Normalize also skips a clip whose waveform hasn't been analysed yet, and a clip that is silent over the part that plays. When nothing in the selection can be normalized, the button and the menu item are disabled, and a press that does nothing beeps.
71	
72	*Agents:* `normalize_clip` (`clips`, optional `peak_db` from −60 to 0, default −1). It answers each clip's `result_db` and lists every skipped clip under `skipped` with the reason.
73	
74	## Fades
75	
76	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
77	|---|---|---|---|
78	| Fade in | How long the sound takes to rise from silence at the clip's start. Quick picks: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 s. | 0–10 s | 0 |
79	| Fade out | How long the sound takes to fall to silence at the clip's end. Same quick picks. | 0–10 s | 0 |
80	
81	In the inspector, a fade length is stored as you type it, not rounded to whole frames. The section summary shows both lengths ("0.50 · 1.00 s"), or "none".
82	
83	A fade is a straight-line ramp in level from silence (fade in) or to silence (fade out), measured from the clip's own edges. It travels with the clip when you move it, and it stays at the edge when you trim. Where a fade in and a fade out overlap, or a fade is longer than the clip, the two multiply, which gives a dip in the middle rather than a jump.
84	
85	### Fade handles on the timeline
86	
87	Every clip with sound has a small square handle at each top corner of its audio area. Drag the left handle inward to set the fade in, or the right handle inward to set the fade out. The handle then sits at the end of the fade.
88	
89	- The fade length snaps to whole frames and can't be longer than the clip.
90	- Fade handles don't snap to clip edges, markers or the playhead, because a fade is a length, not a position.
91	- Each drag is one undo step.
92	- Fade handles don't respond on a locked track.
93	
94	The handles and the inspector rows change the same two settings.
95	
96	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `fade_in` / `fade_out` in ticks.
97	
98	## Ducking
99	
100	Ducking lowers every *other* clip while this one plays. The usual use is to turn on ducking for a voice-over clip so the music drops under it.
101	
102	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
103	|---|---|---|---|
104	| Duck other audio | Turns ducking on for this clip. | on / off | off |
105	| Level | How loud the other clips are while this one plays. Quick picks: 0, 10, 20, 30, 50 %. | 0–100 % | 20 % |
106	| Attack | How long the other clips take to fall to Level, starting from this clip's first frame. Quick picks: 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1 s. | 0–5 s | 0.5 s |
107	| Release | How long they take to come back up, starting after this clip ends. Quick picks: 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 s. | 0–5 s | 1 s |
108	
109	Level, Attack and Release are disabled until ducking is turned on.
110	
111	Attack and Release are stored as you type them, not rounded to whole frames.
112	
113	Ducking follows the clip's length on the timeline, not whether anyone is talking. The other audio stays lowered for the whole length of the ducking clip, through pauses, and comes back up only after the clip ends. You can therefore see exactly when ducking applies by looking at the timeline. If the attack is longer than the clip, the level never fully reaches Level, and the release starts from wherever it got to.
114	
115	- **Overlapping duckers multiply.** Where two ducking clips overlap, their levels multiply: two at 50 % give 25 %.
116	- **A silent ducking clip still ducks.** Ducking is read from the clip's place on the timeline, so a ducking clip that is muted, silenced by a solo, or has its audio switched off still lowers the others. Turn ducking off to stop it.
117	- **Inside a nest**, a ducking clip lowers the rest of the project over the part of it that plays. Ducking on the nest clip itself lowers it over the nest's whole length.
118	
119	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `duck: {level, attack, release}`, or `duck: null` to turn it off.
120	
121	## Noise Reduction
122	
123	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
124	|---|---|---|---|
125	| Remove noise | How much steady background noise to remove. Quick picks: 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 %. | 0–100 % | 0 (off) |
126	| Depth | Read-only: the most any part of the spectrum is turned down, for example "6 dB at most". It reads "floor removed" at 100 % and "off" at 0. | — | off |
127	
128	The noise reducer works out the background noise level from the clip itself, so you don't need to give it a sample of the noise or a stretch of silence. It then turns down whatever sits at that level. It works well on hiss, hum and fan noise.
129	
130	It is not a gate. It doesn't silence the gaps between words, and it can't remove sudden sounds such as a door slam. A long held note may eventually be treated as noise.
131	
132	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `noise_reduction` from 0 to 1.
133	
134	## Compressor
135	
136	The compressor evens out loud and quiet passages by turning down whatever goes above the threshold. Its checkbox is labelled **Smooth volume levels**.
137	
138	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
139	|---|---|---|---|
140	| Smooth volume levels | Turns the compressor on. | on / off | off |
141	| Threshold | The level above which the compressor starts turning the sound down. Quick picks: −30, −24, −18, −12, −6. | −60–0 dB | −18 dB |
142	| Ratio | How strongly it turns down sound above the threshold. 1:1 does nothing; 20:1 acts like a limiter. Quick picks: 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 8, 20. | 1–20 :1 | 3:1 |
143	| Attack | How quickly it reacts when the level rises. Quick picks: 1, 5, 10, 30, 100 ms. | 0–200 ms | 10 ms |
144	| Release | How quickly it lets go when the level falls. Quick picks: 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 ms. | 10–2000 ms | 200 ms |
145	| Makeup | Gain added afterwards to make up what the compressor took away. Quick picks: 0, 3, 6, 12. | 0–24 dB | 0 dB |
146	
147	The defaults are a gentle setting for speech. The section summary shows the ratio ("3.0:1"), or "off".
148	
149	The compressor acts on the clip's sound before the volume, fades and ducking, so moving the Volume slider doesn't change how hard it compresses. If noise reduction is on, it runs before the compressor, which means the threshold is compared against sound that has already been cleaned. Attack and release are measured in milliseconds and aren't rounded to frames.
150	
151	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `compressor: {threshold_db, ratio, attack, release, makeup_db}` (attack and release in ticks), or `compressor: null` to turn it off.
152	
153	## Mix: pan, mono and Detach Audio
154	
155	| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
156	|---|---|---|---|
157	| Pan | Moves a stereo clip's balance left (−) or right (+). Quick picks: −100, −50, 0, 50, 100. | −100 to 100 | 0 |
158	| Position | Read-only: "centre", or the side and amount, for example "left 40". | — | centre |
159	| Mix to mono | Averages all of the clip's channels into one and sends it to every channel. | on / off | off |
160	| Detach Audio | Moves the clip's audio onto its own clip (see below). | — | — |
161	
162	The section summary reads "centre", "mono" or the pan position. Reset sets the pan back to centre and turns mono off.
163	
164	- **On a stereo clip, Pan is a balance control.** At the centre, nothing changes. Moving it one way turns that side up and the other side down, keeping the total power steady. At hard left or hard right, the side it went to is about 3 dB louder than at the centre.
165	- **Pan has no effect on a clip whose source is mono.**
166	- **Turn on Mix to mono as well to get a true pan.** The mono fold happens before the pan, so both channels then carry the same signal and Pan places that one signal anywhere from left to right.
167	- **Mix to mono has no effect on a one-channel source.**
168	
169	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `pan` from −1 to 1 and `mono`.
170	
171	### Detach Audio
172	
173	**Clip ▸ Detach Audio** (⌥⌘D), or the **Detach Audio** button in the Mix section, splits each selected clip's sound onto a clip of its own on the track below. If the clip is already on the bottom track, Frame Job adds a new track underneath for it.
174	
175	- The original clip keeps its picture, and its audio is switched off.
176	- The new clip plays only sound. It has the same file, in point, length and speed as the original, and it keeps the original's audio settings and actions.
177	- After detaching, you can trim, move and adjust the two clips separately.
178	
179	Detach Audio is refused, with the reason given, for a clip that isn't a media clip, a clip whose file has no audio track, and a clip whose audio is already switched off. It's also refused when the track below already has a clip where the new audio clip would go. A new track is added only when the clip is on the bottom track.
180	
181	There is no control that switches a clip's audio back on. To get the original clip's sound back, use Undo, or ask an agent. A clip whose audio is off shows no waveform and no fade handles, and a clip with both its picture and its sound switched off is drawn dimmed.
182	
183	*Agents:* `detach_audio` (`clip`). `set_enabled` (`clip`, `video`, `audio`) turns either half of a clip back on or off.
184	
185	## Keep pitch when the speed changes
186	
187	When a clip plays faster or slower, its sound either keeps its pitch or changes pitch like tape. The **Keep pitch** checkbox is in the Speed section of the Clip sub-tab and is on by default. Above ×12 a clip's audio is left out of the mix. See [Speed](speed.md) for speed changes, speed ramps and how their audio is rendered.
188	
189	*Agents:* `set_audio` with `keep_pitch`, or `set_speed`.
190	
191	## Crossfading audio across a transition
192	
193	When two clips on one track overlap with a transition, the transition can also crossfade their sound. Turn on **Crossfade Audio** in the clip's Transition section. The crossfade keeps the combined loudness steady across the overlap. See [Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).
194	
195	## Muting and soloing tracks
196	
197	Each track header has four toggles: eye (hide video), **speaker (mute audio)**, lock, and **headphones (solo)**. You can also right-click a track header or an empty part of a lane for the track's menu, which has the same toggles with checkmarks.
198	
199	The **Track** menu has the same commands. They act on the track of the first selected clip, or on the front track when nothing is selected:
200	
201	| Command | What it does |
202	|---|---|
203	| **Track ▸ Mute Audio** | Silences every clip on the track. The picture is unaffected. |
204	| **Track ▸ Solo** | Silences every *other* track in the same container. |
205	| **Track ▸ Hide Video** | Hides the track's picture and leaves its sound playing. |
206	
207	How muting and soloing combine:
208	
209	- **Mute always wins.** A track that is both muted and soloed stays silent.
210	- **You can solo several tracks.** All the soloed tracks play, and every track in the same container that isn't soloed is silenced.
211	- **Solo affects only tracks in the same container.** A solo on a timeline track silences the other timeline tracks, and a nest playing on one of them goes silent with it. A solo on a track inside a nest affects only that nest's other tracks.
212	- **Solo silences the others even if the soloed track is empty**, the way a mixer's solo button works.
213	- **Solo and mute affect sound only.**
214	- **Each toggle is one undo step** ("Mute Track", "Solo Track").
215	
216	A clip's own **Mute** (in the Volume section) silences just that clip.
217	
218	*Agents:* `set_track` (`track`, plus `muted`, `solo`, `hidden` or `locked`).
219	
220	## The level meter
221	
222	The level meter is in the timeline bar, just left of the zoom controls. While the timeline plays, it shows the mix you are hearing:
223	
224	- **Two rows**, one per channel, on a −60 to 0 dB scale.
225	- **A solid bar** for the average (RMS) level, with a lighter wash behind it showing the instantaneous peak.
226	- **A peak-hold mark** that stays at the highest recent level for about 1.2 seconds and then falls.
227	- **A clip cell** at the right end of each row. It lights for 2 seconds whenever a sample reaches full scale.
228	
229	The meter includes everything that shapes what you hear: each clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo, and the compressor and other effects. When playback stops, the bars fall back to the floor. If two projects are open, the meter follows the one that is playing. On a very narrow window there isn't room for the meter, so it is hidden.
230	
231	The screen recorder panel has its own meter for the microphone. See [Screen recording](screen-recording.md).
232	
233	## Loudness on export
234	
235	The level meter shows peaks, not loudness. To make an export hit a loudness target, such as integrated LUFS with a true-peak ceiling, use the export sheet's loudness option. Every export reports what its sound measured, whether or not you normalized it. See [Export](export.md).
236	
237	## Synchronize Audio
238	
239	**Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** lines up two or more clips by their sound. The usual case is a camera clip and a separate audio recorder that captured the same moment. Select the clips, each on its own track, and choose the command. One clip, the **anchor**, stays where it is. Every other clip slides along its own track until its sound plays at the same moment as the anchor's.
240	
241	The anchor is chosen this way:
242	
243	1. Among the selected clips that have a picture, the one that starts earliest. If none of them has a picture, all of the clips are considered.
244	2. If two start at the same time, the one on the rearmost track.
245	3. If they are still tied, the one created first.
246	
247	In other words, a camera clip stays put and the recorder moves to it.
248	
249	### What it does
250	
251	- **It matches the sound itself.** Each file's sound is analysed once when it's imported, so differences in gain, microphone and room don't stop a match. When both clips contain enough speech, at least 2 seconds as judged by the on-device voice model, only the speech is compared.
252	- **It searches the trimmed parts first.** Frame Job first looks for a match within the parts of each clip you have trimmed it to. It searches the whole files only if that finds nothing and one of the clips is trimmed. If a recording contains more than one similar stretch, trim the recorder roughly around the camera's sound so it matches the right one.
253	- **It checks the waveforms.** A match is used only if the two waveforms also line up there, as a clear peak within 48 ms. This keeps two takes of the same words from being treated as one recording. The check also fine-tunes the offset to less than a frame.
254	- **It corrects drift.** If two clocks run at slightly different rates, the recorder slowly falls out of sync over a long take. When the clips overlap for at least 60 seconds, Frame Job measures that drift and corrects it by playing the clip at a slightly different speed, at most 0.2 % from ×1. The correction is a plain resample, so the pitch moves very slightly with it. Drift is left alone when it is under 5 ms over the overlap, when it is too small to tell from no drift (under three times its own uncertainty), or when the speed it needs is more than 0.2 % from ×1. The corrected speed appears in the clip's Speed section (for example ×1.0004), with Keep pitch turned off. The command shows no drift figure of its own; that speed is where the correction shows. Like any clip at a speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off, the corrected clip's sound is rendered in the background, so it is briefly silent in the preview after the correction, and again after each trim, split or speed change of it (see [Speed](speed.md)); an export waits for it.
255	- **It trims the head if needed.** If a clip would have to start before 0:00 to line up, it loses just that much from its start instead, and starts at 0:00 in sync. The anchor is never moved or trimmed.
256	- **Moves land on whole frames.** Clips move by a whole number of frames. A whole command is one undo step, named "Synchronize Audio".
257	
258	### The Synchronizing Audio sheet
259	
260	Matching runs in the background while a **Synchronizing Audio** sheet is shown. The sheet has a progress bar and the line "Matching the sound of N clips…". **Cancel** (Escape) closes it and leaves everything as it was. Nothing moves until a match is found. If you change the project while matching is still running, nothing is applied. Frame Job beeps and the inspector says to choose Synchronize Audio again.
261	
262	### Confident and weak matches
263	
264	A match is **confident** when its best candidate is clearly stronger than every other offset: a confidence of at least 10 and at least 1.5 above the next candidate. A confident match is applied straight away.
265	
266	A match is **weak** when no candidate is confident, but the best one within about 3 seconds of where the clip already sits has a confidence of at least 4. Because a weak match might be unrelated sound, it is never applied without asking. A **Weak match** sheet appears, for example:
267	
268	> Weak match: move “record.aifc” 0.80 s earlier (trimming 0.80 s off its head)?
269	
270	A clip that doesn't need to move, only to have its drift corrected, is asked about this way instead:
271	
272	> Weak match: play “record.aifc” at ×1.0004, correcting its drift?
273	
274	When several clips are weak, one sheet lists them all, separated by semicolons.
275	
276	Under the question, the sheet gives the anchor's name, each match's confidence and the rule the match fell short of. **Apply** (the default button) makes every listed change as one undo step. **Cancel** leaves everything as it is.
277	
278	When nothing matches, the command is refused. The refusal names the offsets it did find and their confidences, so you can move the clip near the right one and try again.
279	
280	### When it refuses
281	
282	From the menu, clips in the selection that play no sound (a still, a file with no audio track, a clip with its audio switched off) and nests are left out without a message, and the command needs at least two other clips with sound. To synchronize clips inside a nest, open it (⌘↓) and select them there.
283	
284	Synchronize Audio is all or nothing. If any clip can't be matched, nothing moves. Frame Job beeps and lists every reason at the foot of the inspector. A clip can't be synchronized when it:
285	
286	- has no sound to line up by (its analysis found no sound at all)
287	- is still being analysed. Its sound features or speech haven't been written yet, so try again in a moment.
288	- holds under 2 seconds of sound
289	- plays more than 0.2 % away from ×1
290	- plays at a rate other than its speed setting
291	- plays reversed
292	- ramps its speed (a speed action changes its rate over its length)
293	- would share a track with another clip being synchronized
294	- would never play at the same time as the anchor once lined up
295	- matches the anchor's sound, but the waveforms don't line up there (for example two takes of the same words), so they are not one recording
296	- matches the anchor's sound, but the two share less than 2 seconds of waveform there, too little to confirm it is one recording
297	- would overlap another clip on its own track after the move
298	- would lose so much of its head that less than a frame is left
299	
300	If the clips are already in sync, nothing changes and Frame Job beeps. The menu item is enabled only when at least two selected clips that aren't nests can play sound.
301	
302	*Agents:* `sync_audio` (`clips`, at least two; optional `anchor`; optional `accept_weak`). A weak match answers `moved: false` and lists its clips under `weak`. Call again with `accept_weak: true` only after the person has agreed to that move. The answer reports each clip's offset, confidence, search, drift and trim. Unlike the menu, the tool refuses a nest or a clip that plays no sound by name.
303	
304	## Recording sound into a project
305	
306	The screen recorder can record a microphone with the screen, or record the microphone alone as a voice-over using **Microphone Only**. Either way the voice lands on a new back track named **Microphone**: alongside the picture for a screen recording, or from the playhead for a voice-over. Those clips are ordinary audio clips with all the controls on this page. See [Screen recording](screen-recording.md).
307	
308	## Related tools
309	
310	- **Edit ▸ Paste Attributes** (⌥⌘V) copies the copied clip's look onto every selected clip in one step, including its whole sound setup: volume, mute, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan, mono and Keep pitch. It's the quickest way to give many clips the same treatment. See [Editing](editing.md). *Agents:* `paste_attributes` with `groups: ["audio"]` for the sound alone.
311	- **Remove Silences** and **Remove Filler Words** cut by sound. See [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](cleanup-tools.md).
312	- **Generate Captions** transcribes a clip's audio. See [Captions](captions.md).
313	- **Settings ▸ Playback** holds Background render, which pre-draws graphics frames. It doesn't change the audio output. See [Settings](settings.md).
314	
315	## Limits
316	
317	- Volume tops out at 3200 % (about +30 dB). The slider covers 0–400 %; type in the field for more.
318	- Pan has no effect on a mono source, and Mix to mono has no effect on a one-channel source.
319	- Ducking follows a clip's length on the timeline, not voice activity.
320	- Noise reduction removes steady noise only. It doesn't remove sudden sounds and doesn't gate.
321	- Only volume, Mute and the fades can be animated with an action. Pan, mono, Keep pitch, the compressor, noise reduction and ducking always apply to the whole clip.
322	- On a nest clip, pan, the compressor and noise reduction have no effect. Set them on the clips inside.
323	- No control switches a clip's audio back on after Detach Audio; use Undo.
324	- Above ×12 a clip's audio is left out of the mix ([Speed](speed.md)).
325	- Synchronize Audio corrects drift only up to 0.2 % from ×1. It doesn't work on nests, reversed clips, ramped clips, or clips playing at other rates.
326	- Normalize and Synchronize Audio both need the clip's sound analysis, which runs after import. Until it finishes, those clips are skipped or refused as "still being analysed".
327	# 1. What this is
328	
329	A screencast editor without a recorder — and, since road map 3,
330	a recorder of the SCREEN, and since §11 CAM-1 of a camera beside it or on its
331	own, whose output is ordinary media. Open one or
332	more video files from disk, arrange them on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, trim,
333	split, annotate, animate, and export. Mac only, Apple Silicon, macOS 26+.
334	
335	The bar is a balance: enough to make a real cut with text,
336	shapes, transitions and simple animation, without Final Cut's magnetic
337	timeline, roles, multicam, scopes, or a plugin ecosystem.
338	
339	Deliberate non-goals: multicam, color grading beyond
340	per-clip controls (§11 GR-1: tier 1 of grading — tone, adjustment clips,
341	looks, LUT import, an ungraded switch and one luma waveform — is in, kept by
342	the owner's verdict of 2026-10-10, and tier 2's scopes, colour wheels,
343	curves and qualifiers beside it, GR-10…GR-13; tier 3's HDR→SDR conversion
344	and camera log are in, GR-15, GR-16; the HDR road map's HLG timeline, its
345	HLG, HDR10 and SDR-version deliverables, HDR scopes, the PQ peak, Canon Log
346	2 and 3 and opt-in linear-light blending are in, HD-1…HD-17; a wide-gamut
347	working space for SDR projects is not wanted, GR-20; tier 4's vectorscope zoom,
348	hue curves, the blend between curves of different point counts and the
349	qualifier's cleanup blur are in, GR-24, GR-31…GR-35, while an Offset
350	wheel, a qualifier on picture clips, 1,024-level scopes and a histogram
351	behind the curves are not wanted, GR-27…GR-30), audio beyond what shipped
352	(volume, fades, duck, pan, compressor, noise reduction, peak normalize, the
353	transition crossfade and the export's loudness target — M3 and §11 R5-2; so
354	no EQ, mix buses or Audio Units, while offline voice effects are deferred
355	rather than out), a plugin system (a clip may draw itself from a JavaScript
356	module in its package, road map 10; nothing else is scriptable — §11 G-1),
357	motion blur, stabilisation, optical-flow retiming and auto-reframe (heavy
358	pixel work or ML, outside the compositor's one-pass shape — road map 2 §4),
359	any platform but macOS. **Screen recording was on this list until road map 3
360	reversed it** (§11): the app records a display or a window through
361	ScreenCaptureKit into a file it then imports exactly as File ▸ Open would —
362	paused and resumed from the menu bar, each stretch its own file and its own
363	clip; callouts reconstructed after the fact stay out. **Camera recording
364	was on it too until §11 CAM-1** (road map "camera-recording") reversed it: a
365	camera alone or beside a screen recording, each its own file and clip.
366	
367	**The opening flow is the point.** File > Open on a `.mov` or `.mp4` (or a
368	drop on the Dock icon, or the welcome window's Open Video…) creates an
369	*untitled* project sized to that file, with the file as the first clip on
370	Track 1, ready to cut. Save then writes a `.framejob` package next to the
371	source. The app is also the Alternate handler for movie, audio and image
372	types so Open With… works from the Finder.
373	# Samples
374	
375	Real recordings the owner made for working on Frame Job's handling of real material, as
376	opposed to the synthetic media `tools/proof/` generates with ffmpeg. A proof, a manual
377	check or a decision may name one; each row says what the file is and what it measures, so
378	a change that claims to improve it has a before to compare with.
379	
380	| File | What it is | Measured |
381	|---|---|---|
382	| `Rode-usb-mic.m4a` | Speech recorded on a RØDE USB desktop microphone, 2026-10-30: clean but quiet (spec §11 AU-1). | 30.4 s, AAC-LC mono, 48 kHz; peak −18.6 dBFS (true peak −18.5 dBTP), integrated −44.7 LUFS, LRA 21.1 LU (ffmpeg `volumedetect`, `ebur128=peak=true`) |
383

file.content:
# Audio

Frame Job mixes sound from every clip that has it: a camera clip, an audio-only file, a microphone recording or a nest. Each clip has its own level, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan and mono fold, and each track can be muted or soloed. Two commands do the measuring for you. Normalize sets a clip's level from its loudest moment, and Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by their sound. The preview and the export use the same mix, so what you hear while editing is what gets written.

## Where audio lives

There is only one kind of track. Any track can hold a clip with sound, whether it is a video file, an audio-only file (a voice-over, music, a recorder's take) or a clip you split off with Detach Audio. A clip with sound shows its waveform in the timeline.

The waveform shows the level of the file itself, so moving the Volume slider doesn't redraw it. It's drawn faded when the clip is muted, when its track is muted, or when another track's solo silences it. A track that holds only sound clips is drawn as a shorter lane than a track with pictures.

When the selection includes at least one clip that plays sound, the Clip tab of the inspector shows a **Sound** sub-tab. A clip counts as having sound when its file has an audio track and its audio is switched on, or when it is a nest that holds audio. The Sound sub-tab has six sections, in this order:

1. **Volume**: level, gain read-out, Mute and Normalize
2. **Fades**: fade in and fade out
3. **Ducking**: lowers every other clip while this one plays
4. **Noise Reduction**
5. **Compressor**
6. **Mix**: pan, mix to mono and Detach Audio

Noise Reduction, Compressor and Mix appear in the order the sound passes through them. Volume, the fades and ducking are applied last, like a fader.

Every section header has a summary and a Reset button that appears when the section differs from its default. The summaries read:

| Section | Summary |
|---|---|
| Volume | "muted", "silent" (at 0 %), or the gain, for example "+3.5 dB" |
| Fades | both lengths, for example "0.50 · 1.00 s", or "none" |
| Ducking | the duck level, for example "20%", or "off" |
| Noise Reduction | the amount, for example "50%", or "off" |
| Compressor | the ratio, for example "3.0:1", or "off" |
| Mix | "centre", "mono", or the pan position, for example "left 40" |

 When you change a control with several clips selected, the change goes to all of them. A control whose clips hold different values is marked mixed.

### Sound on a nest

A nest clip has the same Sound sub-tab, but not every control reaches the clips inside it:

- **Volume, Mute and the fades** on a nest clip scale everything inside it. Turning a nest down turns all of it down, and muting it silences all of it.
- **Mix to mono** on a nest clip folds the nest's whole mix.
- **Ducking** on a nest clip lowers the rest of the project for the nest's whole length.
- **Pan, the compressor and noise reduction** set on a nest clip have no effect. Open the nest (⌘↓) and set them on the clips inside.

*Agents:* `set_audio` (`clips`, `patch`) changes any of these properties on one or more clips. Its patch keys are `volume`, `muted`, `fade_in`, `fade_out`, `duck`, `mono`, `keep_pitch`, `pan`, `compressor` and `noise_reduction`. Setting `duck` or `compressor` to null turns it off. `get_project` reads them back.

## Volume

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volume | The clip's level as a percentage. The slider covers 0–400 %; type a higher value in the field, up to 3200 %. Above 400 % the slider's knob stays at the right end. Quick picks: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 400. | 0–3200 % | 100 % |
| Gain | Read-only: the volume in dB (for example "+6.0 dB"), or "silent" at 0 %. | — | +0.0 dB |
| Mute | Silences the clip without changing its volume. | on / off | off |
| Normalize | Sets the volume from the clip's own loudest moment (see below). | — | — |

The section's summary reads "muted", "silent" or the gain in dB. Reset puts the volume back to 100 % and turns Mute off.

You can animate volume, Mute and the fades with actions. While an action is selected, the Volume row, the Mute checkbox and the Fade in and Fade out rows write that action's end state, so a level moves across the action's span. Pan, Mix to mono, Keep pitch, the compressor, noise reduction and ducking can't be animated. They always change the clip's own settings, even with an action selected.

### Normalize

**Normalize** sets each selected clip's volume so that its loudest moment reaches **−1 dBFS**. It's the button in the Volume section, and it's also **Clip ▸ Normalize**.

- **It measures the material, not the mix.** The level is read from the clip's cached waveform over the part of the file that actually plays. The clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo don't affect the reading.
- **It replaces the volume** rather than multiplying it, so pressing it a second time changes nothing (the second press beeps).
- **Each clip gets its own gain.** Normalize doesn't match levels across a selection. However many clips are selected, it is one undo step, named "Normalize".
- **It writes the clip's base level**, even when the playhead is inside an action. With an action selected, the button carries a small boxed "clip" tag to show this.
- **It leaves Mute alone.**
- **It can go past 400 %.** A quiet recording, such as a desktop USB microphone's, is turned up as far as it needs, up to the 3200 % ceiling (about +30 dB). Only a clip whose peak is quieter than about −31 dBFS can't reach −1 dBFS. It is turned up to 3200 % and stops there.

Some clips in a selection are skipped and the rest are still normalized: nests (their level lives in the clips inside them), shapes, titles and silent movies. Normalize also skips a clip whose waveform hasn't been analysed yet, and a clip that is silent over the part that plays. When nothing in the selection can be normalized, the button and the menu item are disabled, and a press that does nothing beeps.

*Agents:* `normalize_clip` (`clips`, optional `peak_db` from −60 to 0, default −1). It answers each clip's `result_db` and lists every skipped clip under `skipped` with the reason.

## Fades

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fade in | How long the sound takes to rise from silence at the clip's start. Quick picks: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 s. | 0–10 s | 0 |
| Fade out | How long the sound takes to fall to silence at the clip's end. Same quick picks. | 0–10 s | 0 |

In the inspector, a fade length is stored as you type it, not rounded to whole frames. The section summary shows both lengths ("0.50 · 1.00 s"), or "none".

A fade is a straight-line ramp in level from silence (fade in) or to silence (fade out), measured from the clip's own edges. It travels with the clip when you move it, and it stays at the edge when you trim. Where a fade in and a fade out overlap, or a fade is longer than the clip, the two multiply, which gives a dip in the middle rather than a jump.

### Fade handles on the timeline

Every clip with sound has a small square handle at each top corner of its audio area. Drag the left handle inward to set the fade in, or the right handle inward to set the fade out. The handle then sits at the end of the fade.

- The fade length snaps to whole frames and can't be longer than the clip.
- Fade handles don't snap to clip edges, markers or the playhead, because a fade is a length, not a position.
- Each drag is one undo step.
- Fade handles don't respond on a locked track.

The handles and the inspector rows change the same two settings.

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `fade_in` / `fade_out` in ticks.

## Ducking

Ducking lowers every *other* clip while this one plays. The usual use is to turn on ducking for a voice-over clip so the music drops under it.

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Duck other audio | Turns ducking on for this clip. | on / off | off |
| Level | How loud the other clips are while this one plays. Quick picks: 0, 10, 20, 30, 50 %. | 0–100 % | 20 % |
| Attack | How long the other clips take to fall to Level, starting from this clip's first frame. Quick picks: 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1 s. | 0–5 s | 0.5 s |
| Release | How long they take to come back up, starting after this clip ends. Quick picks: 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 s. | 0–5 s | 1 s |

Level, Attack and Release are disabled until ducking is turned on.

Attack and Release are stored as you type them, not rounded to whole frames.

Ducking follows the clip's length on the timeline, not whether anyone is talking. The other audio stays lowered for the whole length of the ducking clip, through pauses, and comes back up only after the clip ends. You can therefore see exactly when ducking applies by looking at the timeline. If the attack is longer than the clip, the level never fully reaches Level, and the release starts from wherever it got to.

- **Overlapping duckers multiply.** Where two ducking clips overlap, their levels multiply: two at 50 % give 25 %.
- **A silent ducking clip still ducks.** Ducking is read from the clip's place on the timeline, so a ducking clip that is muted, silenced by a solo, or has its audio switched off still lowers the others. Turn ducking off to stop it.
- **Inside a nest**, a ducking clip lowers the rest of the project over the part of it that plays. Ducking on the nest clip itself lowers it over the nest's whole length.

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `duck: {level, attack, release}`, or `duck: null` to turn it off.

## Noise Reduction

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remove noise | How much steady background noise to remove. Quick picks: 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 %. | 0–100 % | 0 (off) |
| Depth | Read-only: the most any part of the spectrum is turned down, for example "6 dB at most". It reads "floor removed" at 100 % and "off" at 0. | — | off |

The noise reducer works out the background noise level from the clip itself, so you don't need to give it a sample of the noise or a stretch of silence. It then turns down whatever sits at that level. It works well on hiss, hum and fan noise.

It is not a gate. It doesn't silence the gaps between words, and it can't remove sudden sounds such as a door slam. A long held note may eventually be treated as noise.

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `noise_reduction` from 0 to 1.

## Compressor

The compressor evens out loud and quiet passages by turning down whatever goes above the threshold. Its checkbox is labelled **Smooth volume levels**.

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smooth volume levels | Turns the compressor on. | on / off | off |
| Threshold | The level above which the compressor starts turning the sound down. Quick picks: −30, −24, −18, −12, −6. | −60–0 dB | −18 dB |
| Ratio | How strongly it turns down sound above the threshold. 1:1 does nothing; 20:1 acts like a limiter. Quick picks: 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 8, 20. | 1–20 :1 | 3:1 |
| Attack | How quickly it reacts when the level rises. Quick picks: 1, 5, 10, 30, 100 ms. | 0–200 ms | 10 ms |
| Release | How quickly it lets go when the level falls. Quick picks: 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 ms. | 10–2000 ms | 200 ms |
| Makeup | Gain added afterwards to make up what the compressor took away. Quick picks: 0, 3, 6, 12. | 0–24 dB | 0 dB |

The defaults are a gentle setting for speech. The section summary shows the ratio ("3.0:1"), or "off".

The compressor acts on the clip's sound before the volume, fades and ducking, so moving the Volume slider doesn't change how hard it compresses. If noise reduction is on, it runs before the compressor, which means the threshold is compared against sound that has already been cleaned. Attack and release are measured in milliseconds and aren't rounded to frames.

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `compressor: {threshold_db, ratio, attack, release, makeup_db}` (attack and release in ticks), or `compressor: null` to turn it off.

## Mix: pan, mono and Detach Audio

| Control | What it does | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pan | Moves a stereo clip's balance left (−) or right (+). Quick picks: −100, −50, 0, 50, 100. | −100 to 100 | 0 |
| Position | Read-only: "centre", or the side and amount, for example "left 40". | — | centre |
| Mix to mono | Averages all of the clip's channels into one and sends it to every channel. | on / off | off |
| Detach Audio | Moves the clip's audio onto its own clip (see below). | — | — |

The section summary reads "centre", "mono" or the pan position. Reset sets the pan back to centre and turns mono off.

- **On a stereo clip, Pan is a balance control.** At the centre, nothing changes. Moving it one way turns that side up and the other side down, keeping the total power steady. At hard left or hard right, the side it went to is about 3 dB louder than at the centre.
- **Pan has no effect on a clip whose source is mono.**
- **Turn on Mix to mono as well to get a true pan.** The mono fold happens before the pan, so both channels then carry the same signal and Pan places that one signal anywhere from left to right.
- **Mix to mono has no effect on a one-channel source.**

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `pan` from −1 to 1 and `mono`.

### Detach Audio

**Clip ▸ Detach Audio** (⌥⌘D), or the **Detach Audio** button in the Mix section, splits each selected clip's sound onto a clip of its own on the track below. If the clip is already on the bottom track, Frame Job adds a new track underneath for it.

- The original clip keeps its picture, and its audio is switched off.
- The new clip plays only sound. It has the same file, in point, length and speed as the original, and it keeps the original's audio settings and actions.
- After detaching, you can trim, move and adjust the two clips separately.

Detach Audio is refused, with the reason given, for a clip that isn't a media clip, a clip whose file has no audio track, and a clip whose audio is already switched off. It's also refused when the track below already has a clip where the new audio clip would go. A new track is added only when the clip is on the bottom track.

There is no control that switches a clip's audio back on. To get the original clip's sound back, use Undo, or ask an agent. A clip whose audio is off shows no waveform and no fade handles, and a clip with both its picture and its sound switched off is drawn dimmed.

*Agents:* `detach_audio` (`clip`). `set_enabled` (`clip`, `video`, `audio`) turns either half of a clip back on or off.

## Keep pitch when the speed changes

When a clip plays faster or slower, its sound either keeps its pitch or changes pitch like tape. The **Keep pitch** checkbox is in the Speed section of the Clip sub-tab and is on by default. Above ×12 a clip's audio is left out of the mix. See [Speed](speed.md) for speed changes, speed ramps and how their audio is rendered.

*Agents:* `set_audio` with `keep_pitch`, or `set_speed`.

## Crossfading audio across a transition

When two clips on one track overlap with a transition, the transition can also crossfade their sound. Turn on **Crossfade Audio** in the clip's Transition section. The crossfade keeps the combined loudness steady across the overlap. See [Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

## Muting and soloing tracks

Each track header has four toggles: eye (hide video), **speaker (mute audio)**, lock, and **headphones (solo)**. You can also right-click a track header or an empty part of a lane for the track's menu, which has the same toggles with checkmarks.

The **Track** menu has the same commands. They act on the track of the first selected clip, or on the front track when nothing is selected:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Track ▸ Mute Audio** | Silences every clip on the track. The picture is unaffected. |
| **Track ▸ Solo** | Silences every *other* track in the same container. |
| **Track ▸ Hide Video** | Hides the track's picture and leaves its sound playing. |

How muting and soloing combine:

- **Mute always wins.** A track that is both muted and soloed stays silent.
- **You can solo several tracks.** All the soloed tracks play, and every track in the same container that isn't soloed is silenced.
- **Solo affects only tracks in the same container.** A solo on a timeline track silences the other timeline tracks, and a nest playing on one of them goes silent with it. A solo on a track inside a nest affects only that nest's other tracks.
- **Solo silences the others even if the soloed track is empty**, the way a mixer's solo button works.
- **Solo and mute affect sound only.**
- **Each toggle is one undo step** ("Mute Track", "Solo Track").

A clip's own **Mute** (in the Volume section) silences just that clip.

*Agents:* `set_track` (`track`, plus `muted`, `solo`, `hidden` or `locked`).

## The level meter

The level meter is in the timeline bar, just left of the zoom controls. While the timeline plays, it shows the mix you are hearing:

- **Two rows**, one per channel, on a −60 to 0 dB scale.
- **A solid bar** for the average (RMS) level, with a lighter wash behind it showing the instantaneous peak.
- **A peak-hold mark** that stays at the highest recent level for about 1.2 seconds and then falls.
- **A clip cell** at the right end of each row. It lights for 2 seconds whenever a sample reaches full scale.

The meter includes everything that shapes what you hear: each clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo, and the compressor and other effects. When playback stops, the bars fall back to the floor. If two projects are open, the meter follows the one that is playing. On a very narrow window there isn't room for the meter, so it is hidden.

The screen recorder panel has its own meter for the microphone. See [Screen recording](screen-recording.md).

## Loudness on export

The level meter shows peaks, not loudness. To make an export hit a loudness target, such as integrated LUFS with a true-peak ceiling, use the export sheet's loudness option. Every export reports what its sound measured, whether or not you normalized it. See [Export](export.md).

## Synchronize Audio

**Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** lines up two or more clips by their sound. The usual case is a camera clip and a separate audio recorder that captured the same moment. Select the clips, each on its own track, and choose the command. One clip, the **anchor**, stays where it is. Every other clip slides along its own track until its sound plays at the same moment as the anchor's.

The anchor is chosen this way:

1. Among the selected clips that have a picture, the one that starts earliest. If none of them has a picture, all of the clips are considered.
2. If two start at the same time, the one on the rearmost track.
3. If they are still tied, the one created first.

In other words, a camera clip stays put and the recorder moves to it.

### What it does

- **It matches the sound itself.** Each file's sound is analysed once when it's imported, so differences in gain, microphone and room don't stop a match. When both clips contain enough speech, at least 2 seconds as judged by the on-device voice model, only the speech is compared.
- **It searches the trimmed parts first.** Frame Job first looks for a match within the parts of each clip you have trimmed it to. It searches the whole files only if that finds nothing and one of the clips is trimmed. If a recording contains more than one similar stretch, trim the recorder roughly around the camera's sound so it matches the right one.
- **It checks the waveforms.** A match is used only if the two waveforms also line up there, as a clear peak within 48 ms. This keeps two takes of the same words from being treated as one recording. The check also fine-tunes the offset to less than a frame.
- **It corrects drift.** If two clocks run at slightly different rates, the recorder slowly falls out of sync over a long take. When the clips overlap for at least 60 seconds, Frame Job measures that drift and corrects it by playing the clip at a slightly different speed, at most 0.2 % from ×1. The correction is a plain resample, so the pitch moves very slightly with it. Drift is left alone when it is under 5 ms over the overlap, when it is too small to tell from no drift (under three times its own uncertainty), or when the speed it needs is more than 0.2 % from ×1. The corrected speed appears in the clip's Speed section (for example ×1.0004), with Keep pitch turned off. The command shows no drift figure of its own; that speed is where the correction shows. Like any clip at a speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off, the corrected clip's sound is rendered in the background, so it is briefly silent in the preview after the correction, and again after each trim, split or speed change of it (see [Speed](speed.md)); an export waits for it.
- **It trims the head if needed.** If a clip would have to start before 0:00 to line up, it loses just that much from its start instead, and starts at 0:00 in sync. The anchor is never moved or trimmed.
- **Moves land on whole frames.** Clips move by a whole number of frames. A whole command is one undo step, named "Synchronize Audio".

### The Synchronizing Audio sheet

Matching runs in the background while a **Synchronizing Audio** sheet is shown. The sheet has a progress bar and the line "Matching the sound of N clips…". **Cancel** (Escape) closes it and leaves everything as it was. Nothing moves until a match is found. If you change the project while matching is still running, nothing is applied. Frame Job beeps and the inspector says to choose Synchronize Audio again.

### Confident and weak matches

A match is **confident** when its best candidate is clearly stronger than every other offset: a confidence of at least 10 and at least 1.5 above the next candidate. A confident match is applied straight away.

A match is **weak** when no candidate is confident, but the best one within about 3 seconds of where the clip already sits has a confidence of at least 4. Because a weak match might be unrelated sound, it is never applied without asking. A **Weak match** sheet appears, for example:

> Weak match: move “record.aifc” 0.80 s earlier (trimming 0.80 s off its head)?

A clip that doesn't need to move, only to have its drift corrected, is asked about this way instead:

> Weak match: play “record.aifc” at ×1.0004, correcting its drift?

When several clips are weak, one sheet lists them all, separated by semicolons.

Under the question, the sheet gives the anchor's name, each match's confidence and the rule the match fell short of. **Apply** (the default button) makes every listed change as one undo step. **Cancel** leaves everything as it is.

When nothing matches, the command is refused. The refusal names the offsets it did find and their confidences, so you can move the clip near the right one and try again.

### When it refuses

From the menu, clips in the selection that play no sound (a still, a file with no audio track, a clip with its audio switched off) and nests are left out without a message, and the command needs at least two other clips with sound. To synchronize clips inside a nest, open it (⌘↓) and select them there.

Synchronize Audio is all or nothing. If any clip can't be matched, nothing moves. Frame Job beeps and lists every reason at the foot of the inspector. A clip can't be synchronized when it:

- has no sound to line up by (its analysis found no sound at all)
- is still being analysed. Its sound features or speech haven't been written yet, so try again in a moment.
- holds under 2 seconds of sound
- plays more than 0.2 % away from ×1
- plays at a rate other than its speed setting
- plays reversed
- ramps its speed (a speed action changes its rate over its length)
- would share a track with another clip being synchronized
- would never play at the same time as the anchor once lined up
- matches the anchor's sound, but the waveforms don't line up there (for example two takes of the same words), so they are not one recording
- matches the anchor's sound, but the two share less than 2 seconds of waveform there, too little to confirm it is one recording
- would overlap another clip on its own track after the move
- would lose so much of its head that less than a frame is left

If the clips are already in sync, nothing changes and Frame Job beeps. The menu item is enabled only when at least two selected clips that aren't nests can play sound.

*Agents:* `sync_audio` (`clips`, at least two; optional `anchor`; optional `accept_weak`). A weak match answers `moved: false` and lists its clips under `weak`. Call again with `accept_weak: true` only after the person has agreed to that move. The answer reports each clip's offset, confidence, search, drift and trim. Unlike the menu, the tool refuses a nest or a clip that plays no sound by name.

## Recording sound into a project

The screen recorder can record a microphone with the screen, or record the microphone alone as a voice-over using **Microphone Only**. Either way the voice lands on a new back track named **Microphone**: alongside the picture for a screen recording, or from the playhead for a voice-over. Those clips are ordinary audio clips with all the controls on this page. See [Screen recording](screen-recording.md).

## Related tools

- **Edit ▸ Paste Attributes** (⌥⌘V) copies the copied clip's look onto every selected clip in one step, including its whole sound setup: volume, mute, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan, mono and Keep pitch. It's the quickest way to give many clips the same treatment. See [Editing](editing.md). *Agents:* `paste_attributes` with `groups: ["audio"]` for the sound alone.
- **Remove Silences** and **Remove Filler Words** cut by sound. See [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](cleanup-tools.md).
- **Generate Captions** transcribes a clip's audio. See [Captions](captions.md).
- **Settings ▸ Playback** holds Background render, which pre-draws graphics frames. It doesn't change the audio output. See [Settings](settings.md).

## Limits

- Volume tops out at 3200 % (about +30 dB). The slider covers 0–400 %; type in the field for more.
- Pan has no effect on a mono source, and Mix to mono has no effect on a one-channel source.
- Ducking follows a clip's length on the timeline, not voice activity.
- Noise reduction removes steady noise only. It doesn't remove sudden sounds and doesn't gate.
- Only volume, Mute and the fades can be animated with an action. Pan, mono, Keep pitch, the compressor, noise reduction and ducking always apply to the whole clip.
- On a nest clip, pan, the compressor and noise reduction have no effect. Set them on the clips inside.
- No control switches a clip's audio back on after Detach Audio; use Undo.
- Above ×12 a clip's audio is left out of the mix ([Speed](speed.md)).
- Synchronize Audio corrects drift only up to 0.2 % from ×1. It doesn't work on nests, reversed clips, ramped clips, or clips playing at other rates.
- Normalize and Synchronize Audio both need the clip's sound analysis, which runs after import. Until it finishes, those clips are skipped or refused as "still being analysed".
# 1. What this is

A screencast editor without a recorder — and, since road map 3,
a recorder of the SCREEN, and since §11 CAM-1 of a camera beside it or on its
own, whose output is ordinary media. Open one or
more video files from disk, arrange them on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, trim,
split, annotate, animate, and export. Mac only, Apple Silicon, macOS 26+.

The bar is a balance: enough to make a real cut with text,
shapes, transitions and simple animation, without Final Cut's magnetic
timeline, roles, multicam, scopes, or a plugin ecosystem.

Deliberate non-goals: multicam, color grading beyond
per-clip controls (§11 GR-1: tier 1 of grading — tone, adjustment clips,
looks, LUT import, an ungraded switch and one luma waveform — is in, kept by
the owner's verdict of 2026-10-10, and tier 2's scopes, colour wheels,
curves and qualifiers beside it, GR-10…GR-13; tier 3's HDR→SDR conversion
and camera log are in, GR-15, GR-16; the HDR road map's HLG timeline, its
HLG, HDR10 and SDR-version deliverables, HDR scopes, the PQ peak, Canon Log
2 and 3 and opt-in linear-light blending are in, HD-1…HD-17; a wide-gamut
working space for SDR projects is not wanted, GR-20; tier 4's vectorscope zoom,
hue curves, the blend between curves of different point counts and the
qualifier's cleanup blur are in, GR-24, GR-31…GR-35, while an Offset
wheel, a qualifier on picture clips, 1,024-level scopes and a histogram
behind the curves are not wanted, GR-27…GR-30), audio beyond what shipped
(volume, fades, duck, pan, compressor, noise reduction, peak normalize, the
transition crossfade and the export's loudness target — M3 and §11 R5-2; so
no EQ, mix buses or Audio Units, while offline voice effects are deferred
rather than out), a plugin system (a clip may draw itself from a JavaScript
module in its package, road map 10; nothing else is scriptable — §11 G-1),
motion blur, stabilisation, optical-flow retiming and auto-reframe (heavy
pixel work or ML, outside the compositor's one-pass shape — road map 2 §4),
any platform but macOS. **Screen recording was on this list until road map 3
reversed it** (§11): the app records a display or a window through
ScreenCaptureKit into a file it then imports exactly as File ▸ Open would —
paused and resumed from the menu bar, each stretch its own file and its own
clip; callouts reconstructed after the fact stay out. **Camera recording
was on it too until §11 CAM-1** (road map "camera-recording") reversed it: a
camera alone or beside a screen recording, each its own file and clip.

**The opening flow is the point.** File > Open on a `.mov` or `.mp4` (or a
drop on the Dock icon, or the welcome window's Open Video…) creates an
*untitled* project sized to that file, with the file as the first clip on
Track 1, ready to cut. Save then writes a `.framejob` package next to the
source. The app is also the Alternate handler for movie, audio and image
types so Open With… works from the Finder.

Real recordings the owner made for working on Frame Job's handling of real material, as
opposed to the synthetic media `tools/proof/` generates with ffmpeg. A proof, a manual
check or a decision may name one; each row says what the file is and what it measures, so
a change that claims to improve it has a before to compare with.

You choose the format, then the size, frame rate, quality, loudness and range, and the sheet shows what the file will be before anything is written. Exports can run at once behind a progress sheet, or wait in the Export Queue while you keep editing. Every export of a file with sound reports what that sound measured.

For GIF and APNG it adds the frame count: `· 360 frames, no audio`. For **AV1 (MP4)**, **AV1 (WebM)**, **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** a second line estimates how long the export will take: `Estimated time: about 25 s` (in 5-second steps under a minute, then minutes, then hours and minutes). You choose the format, then the size, frame rate, quality, loudness and range, and the sheet shows what the file will be before anything is written. # Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words

Frame Job has two commands for cleaning up a spoken recording such as a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take. **Remove Silences** finds the dead air and cuts it. **Remove Filler Words** finds the ums and uhs and cuts them on the words' own timings. Both show what they would cut before they cut anything, and both make the whole cut as one undo step. An agent can read the same answers, and it can read a clip's transcript to cut false starts.

Both commands are in the **Clip** menu, after **Close Gap**. Neither has a keyboard shortcut.

## How a clean-up cut works

The two commands cut the same way:

- **Preview first.** While the sheet is open, each span it would remove is shaded on the timeline ruler and lanes, and the sheet reads, for example, "23 cuts · removes 00:00:04:12". With nothing to cut it reads "No cuts" and **Remove** is disabled. The shading goes away when the sheet closes.
- **One edit.** **Remove** cuts every span and closes the timeline over each one, all as a single undo step: **Undo Remove Silences** or **Undo Remove Filler Words**. One ⌘Z restores everything.
- **Across the timeline.** A cut is a ripple delete across every **unlocked** track, not just the clips that were analysed, so the picture above a voice-over is cut with it. Locked tracks are neither cut nor moved.
- **Markers stay where they are.** The sheet's footnote says "markers keep their place."
- **Frame-accurate edges.** Each cut's start rounds up to the next frame and its end rounds down. That way a cut can leave up to a frame of room tone behind, but it never clips the start of the next word.
- **Nests and transitions are protected.** A cut never reaches into a nest clip, because a nest always plays from its first frame and cutting into one would strand the rest of it. A cut also never reaches into a transition's overlap or the area around it. To clean up the audio inside a nest, open it first (**Clip ▸ Open Nest**, ⌘↓) and run the command there, or un-nest it (**Clip ▸ Un-nest**, ⇧⌘G). With a nest open, both commands work on the nest's own timeline.
- **The rest of the editor waits.** Playback pauses when a sheet opens, and other editing commands are unavailable until you close it.

## Remove Silences

**Clip ▸ Remove Silences…** opens the Remove Silences sheet. The command is available whenever the timeline has a clip whose sound is switched on.

### What "silent" means

Silence is measured in the **mix**, as you hear it, not in the raw file:

- A clip you have turned down, faded out, ducked, muted, or silenced by soloing another track is quiet. It never keeps a cut from happening.
- A stretch where *every* clip in scope is quiet counts as silent. A music bed under a voice-over therefore keeps the pauses in the speech from being cut, unless you limit the scope to the voice clip (see **In:** below).
- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording; it does not close the gaps you placed between clips. **Clip ▸ Close Gap** does that.
- A muted clip is left out of the analysis entirely. A muted music bed is never read as one long silence covering the whole song.

### Judge by Voice or Level

**Judge by:** picks how a moment is tested.

| Mode | What counts as quiet | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Voice | Nobody is talking. An on-device voice-activity model listens to each media file once and keeps its answer with the project. A quiet microphone isn't mistaken for silence, and a hum isn't mistaken for speech. | Yes |
| Level | The sound in the mix is quieter than the threshold. | Used when the voice model can't be used |

# Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words

Frame Job has two commands for cleaning up a spoken recording such as a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take. **Remove Silences** finds the dead air and cuts it. **Remove Filler Words** finds the ums and uhs and cuts them on the words' own timings. Both show what they would cut before they cut anything, and both make the whole cut as one undo step. An agent can read the same answers, and it can read a clip's transcript to cut false starts.

Both commands are in the **Clip** menu, after **Close Gap**. Neither has a keyboard shortcut.

## How a clean-up cut works

The two commands cut the same way:

- **Preview first.** While the sheet is open, each span it would remove is shaded on the timeline ruler and lanes, and the sheet reads, for example, "23 cuts · removes 00:00:04:12". With nothing to cut it reads "No cuts" and **Remove** is disabled. The shading goes away when the sheet closes.
- **One edit.** **Remove** cuts every span and closes the timeline over each one, all as a single undo step: **Undo Remove Silences** or **Undo Remove Filler Words**. One ⌘Z restores everything.
- **Across the timeline.** A cut is a ripple delete across every **unlocked** track, not just the clips that were analysed, so the picture above a voice-over is cut with it. Locked tracks are neither cut nor moved.
- **Markers stay where they are.** The sheet's footnote says "markers keep their place."
- **Frame-accurate edges.** Each cut's start rounds up to the next frame and its end rounds down. That way a cut can leave up to a frame of room tone behind, but it never clips the start of the next word.
- **Nests and transitions are protected.** A cut never reaches into a nest clip, because a nest always plays from its first frame and cutting into one would strand the rest of it. A cut also never reaches into a transition's overlap or the area around it. To clean up the audio inside a nest, open it first (**Clip ▸ Open Nest**, ⌘↓) and run the command there, or un-nest it (**Clip ▸ Un-nest**, ⇧⌘G). With a nest open, both commands work on the nest's own timeline.
- **The rest of the editor waits.** Playback pauses when a sheet opens, and other editing commands are unavailable until you close it.

## Remove Silences

**Clip ▸ Remove Silences…** opens the Remove Silences sheet. The command is available whenever the timeline has a clip whose sound is switched on.

### What "silent" means

Silence is measured in the **mix**, as you hear it, not in the raw file:

- A clip you have turned down, faded out, ducked, muted, or silenced by soloing another track is quiet. It never keeps a cut from happening.
- A stretch where *every* clip in scope is quiet counts as silent. A music bed under a voice-over therefore keeps the pauses in the speech from being cut, unless you limit the scope to the voice clip (see **In:** below).
- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording; it does not close the gaps you placed between clips. **Clip ▸ Close Gap** does that.
- A muted clip is left out of the analysis entirely. A muted music bed is never read as one long silence covering the whole song.

### Judge by Voice or Level

**Judge by:** picks how a moment is tested.

| Mode | What counts as quiet | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Voice | Nobody is talking. An on-device voice-activity model listens to each media file once and keeps its answer with the project. A quiet microphone isn't mistaken for silence, and a hum isn't mistaken for speech. | Yes |
| Level | The sound in the mix is quieter than the threshold. | Used when the voice model can't be used |

# Effects survey: transitions, effects and filters after Concat

- **Status:** Survey, 2026-09-15. E1 and E2 were built by road map 5
  (`archive/roadmap-5.md`), which overrides this survey wherever
  the two disagree. **E3–E9 were DEFERRED by the user the same day**: "we'll
  eventually add color grading and LUT import, but not now". Nothing from
  E3–E9 is in the tree.
- **Original:** `archive/effects-survey.md` (1629 lines) is the full
  record. "orig §x" below refers to it.
- **Spec decisions:** R5-1 is this survey's D1 (effects are closed
  vocabularies, never a runtime). R5-2..R5-5 and E2-27 came from road map 5
  and cover E1/E2. The survey's D2–D7 are **proposals only**; none is in
  spec §11. A phase that takes one up records it there before writing code.

## Licensing: read this first

**Concat (`~/devel/Concat`) is AGPL-3.0-or-later. Its behaviour was studied,
and none of its code, shaders, chains or colour tables may be carried over.**
The survey read it only through four read-only scout reports written in the
scouts' own words. Nothing may be carried over at design time or at build
time: no Rust, no `effect.wgsl`, no `effect.toml` or FFmpeg filter chain, no
colour matrix, curve table, LUT data or other asset. A builder must not open
those files to "match" a look. Every number a phase needs is Frame Job's own,
chosen against Frame Job's own fixtures. When a phase says "Concat's", it means
the feature a person sees, never how Concat implements it. Concat's
downloaded "Person" matting model (Robust Video Matting) is GPL-3.0, which is
one more reason E9 uses Vision and ships no model. (orig §9, preamble)

## Context

The user asked for a review of Concat's transitions, effects and filters, a
comparison with Frame Job, and designs for the equivalents. Concat is a
Rust/wgpu editor with a Slint UI, sold as a free CapCut replacement.

What the comparison found (orig §2): **Transitions:** Frame Job was already
ahead. Its ten kinds look the same in preview and export, while three of
Concat's seven render as a cut or a dissolve in Concat's own preview;
**Whole families:** Frame Job had obscure regions, spotlight, shadow,
reflection, blend modes, text reveals, and a keyer with a picker and spill.
Concat has none of them; **Breadth:** Concat was ahead, with a 13-slider
Adjust panel, 39 named looks, 27 stylised effects, masks, flip, adjustment
layers, In/Out/Combo clip animations, 20 voice filters and ML background
removal.

The survey designed nine phases, E1–E9, to close the breadth gap, and ran
two spikes (E0) on the Apple frameworks behind the two heaviest phases.

## Decisions

**D1 — No effect runtime; every effect is a closed, versioned vocabulary**
(spec §11 R5-1). Each effect is an enum variant or a struct with ranges. It
is range-checked by `props_check.rs`, carried by the recipe, mirrored by the
MCP catalog and drawn by the one compositor. There is no package format, no
user shader and no expression language.

Rejected: Concat's package runtime, which shows what one costs: every effect
is rendered twice, once by FFmpeg, and the two disagree; fixtures pin filter
strings, not pictures; the UI cannot reach the parameters.

Spec §1's plugin non-goal stands, amended only by road map 10's G-1.
------
