## Voice-overs (Microphone Only)

To record narration over your edit, choose **Microphone Only** in **Source**:

- **System Audio**, **Show Clicks**, **Size** and **Include Frame Job windows** grey out. Their values are kept for next time.
- **Rate** stays live, because it sets the rate of a new project. **Microphone** and **Record Into** stay live too.
- You must choose a microphone. With **Off**, Record says "Microphone Only records the microphone alone — choose a microphone first."
- Only the Microphone permission is checked. Screen Recording isn't needed.

The countdown and the menu-bar item work as they do for a screen recording. Unlike a screen recording, **the panel stays up** while a voice-over records. Its controls lock, the meter stays live, the footnote shows ● or ❚❚ and the elapsed time, Record reads **Stop**, and a **Pause** / **Resume** button appears beside it. If you close the panel, the voice-over carries on. Stop it from the menu-bar item or **File ▸ Stop Recording** (⌥⌘N), and use the welcome window's **New Recording…** button to bring the panel back.

Each stretch between pauses is its own `.m4a` file. In an open project, every file lands on a **new back track named Microphone**, end to end from the playhead, as one **Add Recording** undo step. It never goes on an existing track. As a new project, the first file is the project (1920×1080 at the chosen rate) and later files follow it on its one track.

While a voice-over records, the panel's note shows a refused **Resume** as it happens: the reason appears there and the voice-over stays paused.

If the microphone stops on its own (for example, it's unplugged), the voice-over ends there and what was recorded still lands, with a note.

## The panel's controls

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | What to record. Lists one row per connected display by name, then **Window…** (pick one window), then **Camera** (a camera on its own), then **Microphone Only** (a voice-over with no picture). | The display you used last, else the main display |
| **Include Frame Job windows** | Puts Frame Job's own windows, such as the editor and the preview, into a display recording. When it's off, they're left out of the picture. | Off |
| **Record the camera too** | With a display or **Window…** as the source, also records the chosen camera beside the screen (see [A camera beside the screen](#a-camera-beside-the-screen)). It's greyed out, keeping its value, with **Camera** or **Microphone Only**. | Off |
| **Camera** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, which camera to record: each connected camera by name, or **None connected**. An iPhone used as a Continuity Camera reads "<name> (Continuity Camera)". It's greyed out otherwise. | The camera you used last, else the Mac's preferred camera, then the first built-in camera, then the first one connected |
| **Format** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, the size and frame rate to record at. **Best** comes first and names the camera's best format, for example **Best (1760×1328 at 30 fps)**. Then come the camera's other formats, such as **1920×1080 at 30 fps**: sizes wider than tall first, then square, then taller than wide, each largest first and at its highest frame rate. It's greyed out otherwise. | The format you used last when the chosen camera has it, else Best |
| **Preview** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, a live picture of the chosen camera at the chosen format, under Format. It's shown as the movie will record it: not mirrored, the whole picture fitted inside. The row appears only then. | — |
| **Microphone** | **Off**, or one of the connected microphones. A live level meter sits beside it. | Off |
| **System Audio** | Records what the system plays, as the movie's own stereo 48 kHz sound track. | On |
| **Show Clicks** | Draws a ring around each mouse click. The pointer itself is always recorded. | Off |
| **Rate** | **30 fps** or **60 fps**: the most frames per second the file may hold. It's also the frame rate of a new project made from the recording. | 60 fps |
| **Size** | **Nominal (points)** records the display at its point size. **Best (pixels)** records every pixel, which is twice the points on a Retina display. | Nominal (points) |
| **Record Into** | **New Project**, or any open project by name. | The front project, else New Project |

Under Size, a note shows what you'll get for the chosen display, for example `1728×1117 points · 3456×2234 pixels`. For a picked window it reads "the picked window's own size". For Microphone Only it reads "no picture — the microphone alone". For Camera it names the format the camera records at, for example `1760×1328 at 30 fps — the camera's best format` with Format set to Best, `1920×1080 at 30 fps — the chosen format` with a format chosen, or "no camera connected".

The footnote at the bottom left shows where recordings are saved (for example `saved in ~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings`). While a recording runs, it shows the elapsed time instead.

The panel remembers your choices between uses, including the display, microphone, camera, camera format, switches, rate, size and the Include Frame Job windows and Record the camera too boxes. The camera format is one choice for every camera: a camera that doesn't have the remembered format shows Best. It doesn't remember a picked window, the Camera or Microphone Only source (each lasts for the session only), or Record Into. A display, microphone or camera that is no longer connected falls back to the main display, to Off, or to the default camera. While the panel is up and not recording, the Camera and Microphone lists follow the devices you plug in or take away (a change made during a recording waits for it to end). A camera that's removed falls back to the default camera, and when it comes back it's chosen again with its format. Plugging in or removing a device doesn't change what the panel remembers.

### Record Into
## Files and formats

Recordings are saved in **`~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings/`**, which Frame Job creates the first time it's needed. They're never stored inside the project package. To carry them into the package, use Consolidate (see [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md)).

| File | Name | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Screen recording | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.mov` | QuickTime movie, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), with system audio as one stereo 48 kHz track when System Audio is on |
| Its microphone | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22 (Microphone).m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC, beside the movie |
| Voice-over | `Voice-over 2026-10-02 at 09.15.04.m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC |
| Camera recording | `Camera Recording 2026-10-26 at 17.14.33.mov` | QuickTime movie at the camera's format, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), no sound of its own; its microphone file sits beside it as for a screen recording |

When a name is already taken, Frame Job adds ` (2)`, ` (3)` and so on.

The microphone is always a separate file from system audio, so you can set the level of your voice and the computer's sound independently. Frame Job measures how far apart the two files started and places the microphone clip to match, trimming its head if it started first.

### Frame rate
## Limits

- The panel records displays, single windows, a camera on its own, and a camera beside a display or a window. A camera records at one of its formats at that format's highest frame rate (not at a lower rate within the format's range). The panel places a camera beside the screen in the bottom-right corner; it has no control for another corner, scale or inset. There's no keystroke or callout overlay.
- When a stretch of a screen recording is left out because its movie can't be read, its camera file stays on disk and is named with its other kept files, but it isn't added to the project. Only that stretch's microphone is.
- There's no global shortcut to stop. Use the menu-bar item or the File menu.
- While a screen recording runs, the menu-bar item is the only place to pause or resume besides the File menu. If macOS hides the item, for example behind the notch or in a crowded menu bar, **File ▸ Stop Recording** and **File ▸ Pause Recording** still work.
- A recording longer than 9:59:59 shows a label wider than the item was sized for.
- When a project is already at its track limit, a recording that needs a new track can't be added. The files stay on disk and the note names them.
- If the screen is locked or every display is asleep, no display can be shared, so nothing can be recorded until one wakes.

See also: [Audio](audio.md) for setting the microphone and system-audio levels, [Export](export.md) for writing the finished edit, and [Menus and shortcuts](menus-and-shortcuts.md).
### Keep pitch

Keep pitch belongs to the clip and is on by default.

- **On:** the voice or music keeps its own pitch at the new speed.
- **Off:** the pitch follows the speed, higher when faster and lower when
  slower, like tape or a record. At any rate but ×1 (up to ×12) the clip's
  sound is rendered in the background first, so it is briefly silent in the
  preview after the change (see [Rendered audio](#rendered-audio)).

Keep pitch always applies to the whole clip, even when an action is selected.
It also controls how a speed ramp sounds (see [Rendered audio](#rendered-audio)).
Above ×12 there is no sound either way.

## Speed ramps
### Rendered audio

Two kinds of clip have their sound rendered into a separate file in the
background, saved in the project package: a clip with a speed ramp, and a
clip at a constant speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off. Renders run one
at a time, and a new one starts after each edit that changes the clip's
timing: a ramp, its rate, a trim or a split. Each render covers the whole
clip's sound. Undo and redo render again too, because the file from before
the edit is not kept, so the clip is briefly silent after an undo as well.
How long the silence lasts grows with the clip's length and rate: well under
a second for a 10 s clip, and a few seconds for a minute of ×4.

- **Keep pitch off:** the sound glides smoothly up and down in pitch with the
  rate, like tape, and stays in step with the picture. At a constant speed it
  plays at that speed's tape pitch, sample-exact.
- **Keep pitch on:** the sound keeps its own pitch as the speed changes.
  After a steep slow-down (for example ×2 → ×0.5) it can run up to about
  22 ms behind the picture.

While a clip's sound is still rendering, that clip plays silent in the
preview. An export waits for every render it needs (its progress reads
"Preparing…" during the wait) and never writes that sound silent. If a render
fails, the export fails with "Clip N's retimed audio could not be
rendered: …". A failed render is not tried again while Frame Job stays open:
the clip stays silent and exports that need it keep failing until you change
the clip's timing (which starts a new render) or quit and reopen Frame Job.

## The ×12 question
### E8 — Voice effects (orig §6 E8, §5a; D4)

`audio.voice` is `{kind, amount, pitch −12…12}`, one per clip, with 16
kinds: voice: pitch, high, deep, robot; tone: bass, treble, bright,
telephone, radio; character: lofi, distorted; space: echo, room, hall,
plate, cathedral.

Each kind is a FIXED chain of Apple units: TimePitch, EQ, Distortion, Delay
and Reverb. A new `VoiceRenderer.swift` renders the clip's source WINDOW to
`cache/voiced/<digest>.caf`. The digest covers stamp, reversed, window,
kind, amount, pitch and a chain version.

The render contract, every line of it measured: 48 kHz STEREO, because
reverb given mono aborts the process; an `AVAudioPlayerNode`; schedule →
`start()` → `play()`; fixed 4,096-frame calls; presets through
`auAudioUnit.currentPreset`; every parameter set and clamped; a unit removed
rather than set to wet 0; no TimePitch at 0 semitones; float CAF; per-kind
makeup gain.

Tails are cut at the clip end. `CompositionBuilder` substitutes the file per
clip, and plays DRY while a render is pending.

### E9 — Remove Background (orig §6 E9, §5b; D5)

If the microphone stops on its own (for example, it's unplugged), the voice-over ends there and what was recorded still lands, with a note.

## The panel's controls

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | What to record. Lists one row per connected display by name, then **Window…** (pick one window), then **Camera** (a camera on its own), then **Microphone Only** (a voice-over with no picture). | The display you used last, else the main display |
| **Include Frame Job windows** | Puts Frame Job's own windows, such as the editor and the preview, into a display recording. When it's off, they're left out of the picture. | Off |
| **Record the camera too** | With a display or **Window…** as the source, also records the chosen camera beside the screen (see [A camera beside the screen](#a-camera-beside-the-screen)). It's greyed out, keeping its value, with **Camera** or **Microphone Only**. | Off |
| **Camera** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, which camera to record: each connected camera by name, or **None connected**. An iPhone used as a Continuity Camera reads "<name> (Continuity Camera)". It's greyed out otherwise. | The camera you used last, else the Mac's preferred camera, then the first built-in camera, then the first one connected |
| **Format** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, the size and frame rate to record at. **Best** comes first and names the camera's best format, for example **Best (1760×1328 at 30 fps)**. Then come the camera's other formats, such as **1920×1080 at 30 fps**: sizes wider than tall first, then square, then taller than wide, each largest first and at its highest frame rate. It's greyed out otherwise. | The format you used last when the chosen camera has it, else Best |
| **Preview** | With **Source** set to **Camera**, or with **Record the camera too** ticked, a live picture of the chosen camera at the chosen format, under Format. It's shown as the movie will record it: not mirrored, the whole picture fitted inside. The row appears only then. | — |
| **Microphone** | **Off**, or one of the connected microphones. A live level meter sits beside it. | Off |
| **System Audio** | Records what the system plays, as the movie's own stereo 48 kHz sound track. | On |
| **Show Clicks** | Draws a ring around each mouse click. The pointer itself is always recorded. | Off |
| **Rate** | **30 fps** or **60 fps**: the most frames per second the file may hold. It's also the frame rate of a new project made from the recording. | 60 fps |
| **Size** | **Nominal (points)** records the display at its point size. **Best (pixels)** records every pixel, which is twice the points on a Retina display. | Nominal (points) |
| **Record Into** | **New Project**, or any open project by name. | The front project, else New Project |

Under Size, a note shows what you'll get for the chosen display, for example `1728×1117 points · 3456×2234 pixels`. For a picked window it reads "the picked window's own size". For Microphone Only it reads "no picture — the microphone alone". For Camera it names the format the camera records at, for example `1760×1328 at 30 fps — the camera's best format` with Format set to Best, `1920×1080 at 30 fps — the chosen format` with a format chosen, or "no camera connected".

The footnote at the bottom left shows where recordings are saved (for example `saved in ~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings`). While a recording runs, it shows the elapsed time instead.

The panel remembers your choices between uses, including the display, microphone, camera, camera format, switches, rate, size and the Include Frame Job windows and Record the camera too boxes. The camera format is one choice for every camera: a camera that doesn't have the remembered format shows Best. It doesn't remember a picked window, the Camera or Microphone Only source (each lasts for the session only), or Record Into. A display, microphone or camera that is no longer connected falls back to the main display, to Off, or to the default camera. While the panel is up and not recording, the Camera and Microphone lists follow the devices you plug in or take away (a change made during a recording waits for it to end). A camera that's removed falls back to the default camera, and when it comes back it's chosen again with its format. Plugging in or removing a device doesn't change what the panel remembers.

### Record Into
## Files and formats

Recordings are saved in **`~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings/`**, which Frame Job creates the first time it's needed. They're never stored inside the project package. To carry them into the package, use Consolidate (see [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md)).

| File | Name | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Screen recording | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.mov` | QuickTime movie, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), with system audio as one stereo 48 kHz track when System Audio is on |
| Its microphone | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22 (Microphone).m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC, beside the movie |
| Voice-over | `Voice-over 2026-10-02 at 09.15.04.m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC |
| Camera recording | `Camera Recording 2026-10-26 at 17.14.33.mov` | QuickTime movie at the camera's format, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), no sound of its own; its microphone file sits beside it as for a screen recording |

When a name is already taken, Frame Job adds ` (2)`, ` (3)` and so on.

The microphone is always a separate file from system audio, so you can set the level of your voice and the computer's sound independently. Frame Job measures how far apart the two files started and places the microphone clip to match, trimming its head if it started first.

### Frame rate
## Limits

- The panel records displays, single windows, a camera on its own, and a camera beside a display or a window. A camera records at one of its formats at that format's highest frame rate (not at a lower rate within the format's range). The panel places a camera beside the screen in the bottom-right corner; it has no control for another corner, scale or inset. There's no keystroke or callout overlay.
- When a stretch of a screen recording is left out because its movie can't be read, its camera file stays on disk and is named with its other kept files, but it isn't added to the project. Only that stretch's microphone is.
- There's no global shortcut to stop. Use the menu-bar item or the File menu.
- While a screen recording runs, the menu-bar item is the only place to pause or resume besides the File menu. If macOS hides the item, for example behind the notch or in a crowded menu bar, **File ▸ Stop Recording** and **File ▸ Pause Recording** still work.
- A recording longer than 9:59:59 shows a label wider than the item was sized for.
- When a project is already at its track limit, a recording that needs a new track can't be added. The files stay on disk and the note names them.
- If the screen is locked or every display is asleep, no display can be shared, so nothing can be recorded until one wakes.

See also: [Audio](audio.md) for setting the microphone and system-audio levels, [Export](export.md) for writing the finished edit, and [Menus and shortcuts](menus-and-shortcuts.md).
### Keep pitch

Keep pitch belongs to the clip and is on by default.

- **On:** the voice or music keeps its own pitch at the new speed.
- **Off:** the pitch follows the speed, higher when faster and lower when
  slower, like tape or a record. At any rate but ×1 (up to ×12) the clip's
  sound is rendered in the background first, so it is briefly silent in the
  preview after the change (see [Rendered audio](#rendered-audio)).

Keep pitch always applies to the whole clip, even when an action is selected.
It also controls how a speed ramp sounds (see [Rendered audio](#rendered-audio)).
Above ×12 there is no sound either way.

## Speed ramps
### Rendered audio

Two kinds of clip have their sound rendered into a separate file in the
background, saved in the project package: a clip with a speed ramp, and a
clip at a constant speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off. Renders run one
at a time, and a new one starts after each edit that changes the clip's
timing: a ramp, its rate, a trim or a split. Each render covers the whole
clip's sound. Undo and redo render again too, because the file from before
the edit is not kept, so the clip is briefly silent after an undo as well.
How long the silence lasts grows with the clip's length and rate: well under
a second for a 10 s clip, and a few seconds for a minute of ×4.

- **Keep pitch off:** the sound glides smoothly up and down in pitch with the
  rate, like tape, and stays in step with the picture. At a constant speed it
  plays at that speed's tape pitch, sample-exact.
- **Keep pitch on:** the sound keeps its own pitch as the speed changes.
  After a steep slow-down (for example ×2 → ×0.5) it can run up to about
  22 ms behind the picture.

While a clip's sound is still rendering, that clip plays silent in the
preview. An export waits for every render it needs (its progress reads
"Preparing…" during the wait) and never writes that sound silent. If a render
fails, the export fails with "Clip N's retimed audio could not be
rendered: …". A failed render is not tried again while Frame Job stays open:
the clip stays silent and exports that need it keep failing until you change
the clip's timing (which starts a new render) or quit and reopen Frame Job.

## The ×12 question
### E8 — Voice effects (orig §6 E8, §5a; D4)

`audio.voice` is `{kind, amount, pitch −12…12}`, one per clip, with 16
kinds: voice: pitch, high, deep, robot; tone: bass, treble, bright,
telephone, radio; character: lofi, distorted; space: echo, room, hall,
plate, cathedral.

Each kind is a FIXED chain of Apple units: TimePitch, EQ, Distortion, Delay
and Reverb. A new `VoiceRenderer.swift` renders the clip's source WINDOW to
`cache/voiced/<digest>.caf`. The digest covers stamp, reversed, window,
kind, amount, pitch and a chain version.

The render contract, every line of it measured: 48 kHz STEREO, because
reverb given mono aborts the process; an `AVAudioPlayerNode`; schedule →
`start()` → `play()`; fixed 4,096-frame calls; presets through
`auAudioUnit.currentPreset`; every parameter set and clamped; a unit removed
rather than set to wet 0; no TimePitch at 0 semitones; float CAF; per-kind
makeup gain.

Tails are cut at the clip end. `CompositionBuilder` substitutes the file per
clip, and plays DRY while a render is pending.

### E9 — Remove Background (orig §6 E9, §5b; D5)

The Final Cut Pro for Mac guide covers the four enhancements you asked about, plus Equalization. The main page is at Apple's "Enhance audio" article, and its sections are summarized below.

- **Voice Isolation** gives priority to detectable human voices. Running it on several simultaneous audio components can produce garbled sound, and turning it off for some of them is the suggested fix. Voice Isolation prioritizes any detectable human voices over other parts of the audio signal. Turning on Voice Isolation for several audio components that are all playing at the same time may result in garbled audio. If this occurs, try turning off Voice Isolation for one or more audio components.
- **Loudness** has two sliders. Amount controls overall compression, and Uniformity controls which dynamic range is affected (Amount and Uniformity sliders in the Loudness section. The Amount slider adjusts the overall loudness (compression) of the clip, and the Uniformity slider adjusts the dynamic range affected.).
- **Noise Removal** is adjusted with an Amount slider in its section (Drag the Amount slider in the Noise Removal section.).
- **Hum Removal** lets you pick 50 Hz or 60 Hz, which matches local mains frequency (Select either 50 Hz or 60 Hz in the Hum Removal section.).

Equalization and Voice Isolation are not on by default. Equalization and Voice Isolation must be turned on manually in the Audio Enhancements section of the Audio inspector. Enhancements also apply per component, not per clip. Audio enhancement works on the component level, not the clip level.

For automatic correction, choose Modify > Enhance Audio (or press Option-Command-A). A yellow warning triangle in the inspector can flag potential problems.

Caveat: the search metadata shows these Mac pages as about 1,623 days old, so control names may differ in the current version. The iPad guide describes Noise Removal as covering background hissing, buzzing, and humming, and it has no separate Hum Removal control. I did not check the current version, so verify against the live guide if the exact labels matter.

- **Loudness** has two sliders. Amount controls overall compression, and Uniformity controls which dynamic range is affected (Amount and Uniformity sliders in the Loudness section. The Amount slider adjusts the overall loudness (compression) of the clip, and the Uniformity slider adjusts the dynamic range affected.).

Adobe's help pages cover all three features in the Essential Sound panel, though the pages vary in age.

- **Auto-Match loudness:** Adobe says Auto-Match adjusts clips toward a level suited to their audio type, so you should tag audio types first. The clip's LUFS value appears under the button ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/auto-match-audio-loudness.html)). For a whole track, one guide describes using Auto-Match to bring every clip of that type to a standard level ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/ph_fil/premiere-pro/how-to/create-audio-mix.html)).
- **Auto Ducking:** You assign audio types, then choose which types to duck against (Dialogue, Music, Sound Effects, Ambience, or untagged). Sensitivity, Duck Amount, Fade Duration, and Fade Position control the result ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/africa/premiere-pro/using/auto-ducking.html), [helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/automatically-duck-audio.html)). Ducking adds an Amplify effect, and its keyframes go on the gain parameter, so they can be edited without touching other sound design ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/automatically-duck-audio.html)). Each new Generate Keyframes run replaces the earlier keyframes ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/ph_fil/premiere-pro/how-to/automatic-audio-ducking.html)).
- **Enhance Speech:** This is an AI tool for dialogue clips that reduces background noise and improves vocal clarity. You select the clip and click Enhance in the panel. It runs in the background with a progress bar, and a Mix Amount slider blends the result with the original ([helpx.adobe.com](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/enhance-speech.html)).

The ducking page dated about 1,400 days ago is the oldest of these, so its interface may be out of date. The other pages are about 300 to 700 days old. I didn't find any sources on Premiere version changes or on how these tools compare to Adobe's newer audio features.

I ran one search. It didn't return the Resolve 20 Reference Manual's pages for these tools, so the results below come from Blackmagic's feature guides, the product page, and user forum threads.

- **Voice Isolation and Dialogue Leveler:** Blackmagic's Resolve 20 New Features Guide describes them as tools that help you get usable results from weak microphones and poor recording rooms. Voice Isolation reduces background noise while you record, and Dialog Leveler keeps the track at a steady volume. These are clip-level effects in the Inspector, and the Clip Inspector shows the Voice Isolation and Voice Leveller modules below the Pan module, and both start out bypassed and minimized.
- **Track-level placement:** Users report that the same effects can also be added to whole tracks through the Fairlight mixer's Track FX menu. One forum poster says applying voice isolation in Fairlight at the track or group level is more reliable than using the Inspector. That's anecdotal, so check it yourself.
- **Ducker:** Blackmagic's Fairlight page describes it as lowering a music track while dialogue plays. The track FX ducker plug-in uses the signal from one or more dialogue tracks to automatically control volume reduction on a target track. A forum thread reports that in Resolve 20, Auto Ducking does not write its gain changes into Fader Level automation, and Resolve 20 keeps these two systems separate.
- **Manual wording:** A forum user says the manual's description of these tools says they support "any mono or stereo (or multi-mono) audio track, but is not supported on greater-than-stereo tracks."
- **Manual status:** The Resolve 20.2 New Features Guide says these changes will be included in the next update of the full DaVinci Resolve Reference Manual. So for exact current settings, the Resolve 20.x manual may lag behind the release notes.

Adobe's help pages describe the Essential Sound panel's Repair and Clarity sections, which match the controls in your query.

**Repair section (dialogue):** Each control has a checkbox and a 0–10 slider.
- **Reduce Noise** targets background hiss, mic noise, and clicks. The right amount depends on how much signal loss you can accept ([helpx.adobe.com, item 1](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/repair-dialogue.html)).
- **Reduce Rumble** addresses very low-frequency noise below about 80 Hz, such as motor vibration ([item 1](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/repair-dialogue.html)).
- **DeHum** removes mains hum at 50 Hz or 60 Hz, depending on region ([item 5](https://helpx.adobe.com/audition/desktop/editing-audio-files/essential-sound-panel.html)).
- **DeEss** reduces harsh sibilant "s" sounds ([item 5](https://helpx.adobe.com/audition/desktop/editing-audio-files/essential-sound-panel.html)).
- **Reduce Reverb** cuts room reflections so the voice sounds like it comes from one source ([item 1](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/repair-dialogue.html)).

Enabling Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb applies DeNoise and DeReverb effects to the clip, and their advanced settings are in the Effect Controls panel ([item 9](https://helpx.adobe.com/ph_fil/premiere-pro/how-to/advanced-noise-reverberation-reduction.html)). Removing noise or reverb often lowers clip loudness, so you may need to compensate with the clip volume control ([item 2](https://helpx.adobe.com/ph_fil/premiere-pro/how-to/reduce-noise-and-reverberation.html)).

**Clarity section:**
- **Dynamics** shifts the recording between a more natural sound and a more compressed, focused one ([item 6](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/improve-dialogue-clarity.html)). High settings can distort vocals ([item 10](https://helpx.adobe.com/ph_fil/premiere-pro/how-to/improve-audio-quality.html)).
- **EQ** boosts or cuts chosen frequencies using a preset and an amount slider ([item 6](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/add-audio-effects/adjust-volume-and-levels/improve-dialogue-clarity.html)).

Note that these pages are Adobe's own help documentation, and some are dated (the newest was about 296 days old in these results). Control names and layouts may differ in your Premiere version.

The search turned up Adobe's help pages on the Audio Track Mixer. Key points:

- **Submixes and sends:** A submix combines signals from selected tracks and sits between those tracks and the master. Sends are often used to route a track's signal to a submix track for effects processing. Each track has five sends, and a send can be set pre-fader or post-fader (each track contains five sends, located in the Effects And Sends panel).
- **Effects:** Effects go into slots in the Track Effects panel, and multiple effects can run at once (Reverb, Amplitude, and Compression can be applied to entire tracks).
- **Automation modes:** Adobe describes Off, Read, Latch, Touch, and Write. Latch starts recording when a control is adjusted and holds the new value until playback stops. Touch records only while a control is held, then returns to the prior value. Write records continuously during playback. Write mode also has a switch-to-Touch option after playback (the Switch To Touch After Write command switches all Write mode tracks to Touch mode). The return speed for Touch and Read is set by the Automatch Time preference.
- **Known issue:** Adobe's September 2026 release notes (version 26.5) list a bug where the Audio Track Mixer's "Write" automation mode did not work. Check whether it's fixed before relying on Write.
- **Clip vs. track mixer:** The Audio Clip Mixer offers only Touch and Latch, and it records clip keyframes rather than track keyframes (these modes are available only in the Audio Clip Mixer and work with clips under the playhead. For track-level automation that affects entire audio tracks rather than individual clips, use the Audio Track Mixer instead.)

Adobe's documentation covers Remix in Premiere Pro, which retimes music to a target length through the Essential Sound panel.

- **How it works:** Remix uses AI-based beat analysis to find cut points and loops, and it keeps the opening and closing of the track while reworking the middle. Remix analyzes the musical structure of your audio clip by measuring qualities of each beat and comparing them across the entire song. The tool then identifies the optimal cut points and loops to create a musically coherent version at your target duration, complete with automatic crossfades.
- **Setting duration:** You can drag the right edge of a music clip with the Remix Tool, or type a value into Target Duration in the Essential Sound panel. (1-10, 1-11, 1-12)
- **Accuracy:** Adobe's figures differ by page. One says the Remix tool finds a version of your music within 5 seconds of the target duration, typically within 1 second. Another says results usually land within one second of your target duration. Accuracy depends on original tempo and composition, available transition points in the song structure, and the number of distinct musical sections.
- **Tuning controls:** Segments controls how many cuts and crossfades are used. Variations shifts emphasis between melodic and harmonic elements. (4-10)
- **Preview caveat:** Adobe notes a slight timing issue with preview versions of Adobe Stock music. If you use Remix on a Preview and then decide to purchase the track, check the timing of your remix with the full version.
- **Older/alternate workflow:** Audition's Remix tool can handle the same job via Edit In Adobe Audition, and Premiere Elements has its own Music Remix feature with a similar remix-handle approach. (5-8, 8-6)

The official Adobe help pages cover all five effects. Loudness Radar has been superseded by Loudness Meter in newer versions.

- **Loudness Radar:** Adobe's help pages describe it as a way to measure a sequence's loudness without altering the audio, so you can adjust levels based on its readings. The Loudness Radar effect does not change the audio level. It gives you a precise measure of Loudness that you can use to change your audio loudness levels. Newer releases favor Loudness Meter, and the older Radar is kept for projects from versions earlier than 15.2.
- **Hard Limiter:** It caps peaks above a set threshold. Adobe's library notes that it is typically paired with an input boost to raise overall volume without distortion (The effect greatly attenuates audio that rises above a specified threshold. Typically, limiting is applied with an input boost).
- **DeNoise:** It reduces background noise such as hum, hiss, and fans, with a slider controlling the amount (The DeNoise effect reduces or completely removes noise from your audio file. This noise could be unwanted hum and hiss, fans, air conditioner, or any other background noise. You can control the amount of noise reduced using a slider.).
- **DeReverb:** It estimates the room's reverberation and lets you adjust how much is removed, on a 0–100% scale (The DeReverb effect estimates the reverberation profile and helps adjust the reverberation amount. The values range from 0% to 100%).
- **Parametric Equalizer:** It offers detailed control over frequency, Q, and gain. Adobe's reference lists up to five intermediate bands plus high-pass, low-pass, and shelving filters, and notes that high Q values suit notch filtering such as removing 60 Hz hum (High Q values (close to 100) affect a narrow band and are ideal for notch filters removing particular frequencies, like 60-Hz hum.).

Adobe's Essential Sound panel also applies DeNoise and DeReverb automatically through its Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb switches, and the Effect Controls panel exposes the advanced settings (When you enable Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb in the Essential Sound panel, DeNoise and DeReverb effects are applied to selected clips respectively.).

Main sources: Adobe's "Audio effects and transitions" (helpx.adobe.com/se/premiere-pro/using/audio-effects-transitions.html), the "Apply audio effects in Premiere" library page, and the Loudness Meter and Advanced noise and reverb reduction help pages.

Newer releases favor Loudness Meter, and the older Radar is kept for projects from versions earlier than 15.2.
- **Hard Limiter:** It caps peaks above a set threshold. Adobe's library notes that it is typically paired with an input boost to raise overall volume without distortion (The effect greatly attenuates audio that rises above a specified threshold. Typically, limiting is applied with an input boost).
- **DeNoise:** It reduces background noise such as hum, hiss, and fans, with a slider controlling the amount (The DeNoise effect reduces or completely removes noise from your audio file. This noise could be unwanted hum and hiss, fans, air conditioner, or any other background noise. You can control the amount of noise reduced using a slider.).
- **DeReverb:** It estimates the room's reverberation and lets you adjust how much is removed, on a 0–100% scale (The DeReverb effect estimates the reverberation profile and helps adjust the reverberation amount. The values range from 0% to 100%).
- **Parametric Equalizer:** It offers detailed control over frequency, Q, and gain. Adobe's reference lists up to five intermediate bands plus high-pass, low-pass, and shelving filters, and notes that high Q values suit notch filtering such as removing 60 Hz hum (High Q values (close to 100) affect a narrow band and are ideal for notch filters removing particular frequencies, like 60-Hz hum.).

Adobe's Essential Sound panel also applies DeNoise and DeReverb automatically through its Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb switches, and the Effect Controls panel exposes the advanced settings (When you enable Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb in the Essential Sound panel, DeNoise and DeReverb effects are applied to selected clips respectively.).

The search turned up Adobe's documentation on loudness normalization at export, though it's written for Media Encoder, which is where Premiere's export settings hand off.

**Setup at export:** Adobe's guide describes enabling Loudness Normalization in the Effects tab and picking a standard from the dropdown. The options are ATSC A/85, EBU R128, and ITU BS.1770-3, and you can only change the loudness for ITU BS.1770-3. You cannot change the loudness for the other standards.

**True peak:** To control overshoots more tightly, you can select the Configure True Peak Limiter checkbox, then set the Look-Ahead Time and Release Time values for the limiter. Per the same guide, Media Encoder then normalizes the audio to the chosen standard and applies those limiter settings.

**Reports:** Checking Write Loudness Report saves an XML file with the loudness value and true peak level alongside the export.

**Channel layouts:** Normalization works natively with mono, stereo, and 5.1. Other layouts such as 4ch or 8ch trigger a Channel Configuration screen, and the channel counts you assign must match the source file's channel count.

**Measuring in Premiere:** The Loudness Meter effect offers presets for regional and platform targets, and its settings include a Maximum True Peak value. Maximum True Peak · Sets the maximum True Peak level. The peak indicator is activated if the signal is above 0dBTP. The older Loudness Radar effect uses BS.1770-3 with Leq(K) measurement, per Adobe's documentation.

**Caveat:** The results don't include a page confirming the exact export-panel path in current Premiere versions, so verify the Effects tab location in your build. The documentation I found is also dated, with some pages more than four years old.

Adobe's help pages cover the basics of audio keyframes and the rubber band in Premiere Pro.

- **Turning on the display:** Adobe says to enable Show Audio Keyframes in the Timeline settings menu, and to make the audio track taller if the line is hard to see (help.adobe.com, Record a voice over, results 1-12 and 1-34/1-35).
- **Adding keyframes with the Pen tool:** Select the Pen tool, then click the thin line on the clip to add a keyframe. Dragging it up raises the volume and dragging it down lowers it, and dragging sideways moves when the change happens (results 1-37 to 1-41).
- **Editing and deleting:** The Pen tool can lasso several keyframes to move or delete them together. Adobe recommends switching back to the Selection tool when you finish (results 1-44 and 1-47).
- **Clip versus track keyframes:** Clip keyframes stay with the clip, so they move if you drag the clip. Track keyframes apply to the whole track and are not limited to clip boundaries (results 2-56 to 2-59 and 4-5).
- **Track volume:** Track-level adjustments are separate from clip adjustments, so moving or replacing clips does not affect them (result 4-3).
- **Pen tool description:** Adobe's Tools panel page describes the Pen tool as the tool for setting or selecting keyframes, and says Ctrl-click or Command-click on the connector line adds one (result 9-8 to 9-10).

Sources differ on minor details. One page says Ctrl/Command-click creates keyframes, while another says the Pen tool does, and they describe the controls for the Audio Track Mixer differently. The search didn't turn up anything specific to exporting stems from Premiere Pro. It did cover how to remap channels and how export channel settings behave.

- **Remapping clip channels:** You can select clips in the Project panel and open Modify > Audio Channels. There, a matrix lets you choose which clip channel feeds which source channel. The Audio Channels dialog box shows clip channels on the left and source channels across the top, and selecting a cell maps one to the other. Adobe's help notes that proxies can cause unexpected behavior if your workflow depends on Modify Audio Channels.
- **Disabling channels:** You can turn individual channels off. Only the enabled channels get added to the Timeline when you place a clip in a sequence.
- **Export channel layout:** The export's Audio channel setting controls the output layout. If you pick fewer channels than the sequence's Mix track or media file has, Premiere downmixes the audio. Downmixing only works for certain combinations, such as 5.1 to stereo or stereo to mono, not N-channel to stereo or mono.
- **Splitting to mono:** The Breakout To Mono command creates mono audio source clips from a clip's stereo or 5.1 surround channels. Adobe's notes say the Source Channel Mappings command creates linked mono clips.
- **Sequence routing:** For multichannel masters, the Audio Track Mixer's Direct Output Assignment button controls which master channels each track feeds. You pick the destination master channel by marking the matrix.

The search turned up Apple's Final Cut Pro for Mac user guide pages on audio channels and components. The main points:

- **Components:** Final Cut Pro groups a clip's audio channels into components based on how the channels are configured, and you can expand the audio to edit each component separately. It groups channels automatically, and expanding the audio portion lets you work on components down to the individual channel level.
- **Changing the configuration:** In the Audio inspector's Audio Configuration section, the Channels pop-up menu sets the layout. Available formats include mono, stereo, and 5.1 surround (configurable as mono, stereo, or surround). Switching layouts resets edits made to the components, so do it before fine-tuning.
- **Enabling or disabling components:** Checkboxes beside each waveform in the Audio inspector turn components on or off. Turning one off removes it from the clip's arrangement in the timeline.
- **Expanding in the timeline:** Choosing Clip > Expand Audio Components (or pressing Control-Option-S) shows the components in the timeline. Apple's multichannel editing examples describe this same command.
- **File format caveat:** Compressed stereo formats such as AAC and MP3 are usually interleaved, so they appear as one component until you change the clip's channel configuration.

The Apple support results cover Final Cut Pro's built-in level metering and the MultiMeter effect's loudness tools.

**Built-in audio meters:** The main Apple guide describes meters that show clip levels and flag peaks that could cause distortion. Meter colors shift as a clip nears peak and again when it passes it. The peak indicators reset when playback stops and starts again. The meters can be shown from the Window menu or the icon below the viewer, and they can be expanded by dragging their edges. ([Apple, View and change audio levels](https://support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro/view-and-change-audio-levels-verc1faad4f/mac))

**Volume adjustment:** The Adjust Volume guide recommends using the meters to keep volume below peak levels. Clip volume can be changed by dragging the line on the waveform, or with the Modify menu in +1/–1 dB steps or absolute dB values. ([Apple, Adjust volume](https://support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro/adjust-volume-verc1fabb77/mac))

**MultiMeter effect (Logic effects):** This effect offers a Level meter with selectable Peak, RMS, and True Peak modes, plus peak hold and a reset option. Its Loudness meter follows the AES 128 specification and reports values in LUFS, with LU-I (integrated) and LU-S (short-term) readouts. Other tools include an Analyzer, a Goniometer, and a Correlation meter. ([Apple, MultiMeter Level and Loudness](https://support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro-logic-effects/level-and-loudness-controls-lgex1d0722a3/mac); [Apple, Intro to MultiMeter](https://support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro-logic-effects/intro-to-multimeter-lgexd99fdf3c/mac))

**Limiting:** The Adaptive Limiter and Limiter effects have input, reduction, and output meters with margin fields that show peak values. Apple says Adaptive Limiter is typically used on the final mix. ([Apple, Adaptive Limiter](https://support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro-logic-effects/adaptive-limiter-lgex931a149c/mac))

The search returned no information on loudness targets (such as a specific LUFS delivery standard) or on the meter's on-screen loudness readout in the built-in meters, so those would need a separate search.

The guide describes three formats: Mono, Stereo, and 5.1 surround. It does not mention Dual Mono. The number of options you get depends on how many channels the source clip or compound clip contains.

- **Mono:** "Single channel." In surround setups, a mono channel can be assigned to any surround channel.

- **5.1 surround:** "Left, center, right, left surround, right surround, and low-frequency effects (subwoofer bass) channels."

If a clip has more than six surround channels, Final Cut Pro mixes it down to 5.1 during playback: "Final Cut Pro automatically adjusts the channel mix down to 5.1 surround during playback."

- You can skim or play each component to hear it.

- Changing the channel configuration has a side effect: "Changing the channel configuration resets all adjustments and edits made to audio components." This includes applied effects, disabled ranges, keyframe adjustments, and role assignments.

content.content:
**Sources of effects**
- Final Cut Pro includes a range of custom effects and Logic effects, which are digital signal processing (DSP) tools. Quote: "Final Cut Pro also comes with an extensive range of custom audio effects and professional Logic effects" (about 105 characters).
- You can also use macOS built-in and third-party Audio Units. Quote: "you can take advantage of 64-bit macOS built-in and third-party Audio Units (AU) effects" (about 90 characters).

**Where effects are applied**
- Effects can go on individual clips, their components, or compound clips. Quote: "You can add effects to individual audio clips and components or to a compound clip." (about 85 characters)
- To apply one, select an effect in the Effects browser and drag it onto a clip, or double-click it to apply it to the selected clip.
- The page does not discuss roles as a way to apply effects.

**Effect order**
- Effects process audio in the order they're listed, and that order changes the result. Quote: "The order in which you apply them affects the final output." (about 60 characters)
- The page's example is a reverb followed by a Noise Gate, where the gate may treat reverb as noise.
- The page suggests applying noise reduction first, then EQ or special effects, then compression or limiters.
- You can reorder effects by dragging them in the Audio inspector or the Audio Animation editor.

**Adjusting and keyframing**
- After adding an effect, you adjust its settings in the Audio inspector. Quote: "After you add an effect, you can adjust its settings using the Audio inspector." (about 80 characters)
- Effects also appear in the Audio Animation editor.
- The page mentions keyframe adjustments only in the context of copying attributes between clips. It does not explain how to keyframe effect parameters.

**Copying effects and presets**
- You can copy all of a clip's effects to another clip with Edit > Copy and Edit > Paste Effects.
- You can also paste selected attributes, including effects and keyframe adjustments, using Paste Attributes.
- The page does not cover saving or applying effect presets. The table of contents links to a separate "Save audio effects presets" topic, which this page doesn't include.

- **Fade handles and crossfades:** Modify > Adjust Audio Fades > Crossfade (Option-T) adds a crossfade at an edit point automatically. Apple's Final Cut Pro guide covers this in its Match Audio instructions.

- **What it does:** Apple's page on the Match Audio function uses equalization (EQ) to let you match a selected clip's sound to that of another clip. It's most useful when you have multiple audio clips recorded in different environments but want the clips to sound similar.
- **Steps:** Select the clip(s) to change in the timeline. Then choose Modify > Match Audio (Shift-Command-M), or pick Match from the Equalization pop-up in the Audio Enhancements section of the Audio inspector. Next, click the clip whose sound you want to copy, and click Apply Match (1-4, 1-5, 1-13, 1-14, 1-15).
- **Component-level selection:** For clips with several components, such as dual mono, compound, multicam, or synced clips, Apple says the selection must be made at the component level.
- **Adjusting or undoing:** After matching, you can fine-tune the settings in the Audio Enhancements section of the Audio inspector. To remove the match, pick a different equalization setting, or choose Flat to remove all equalization (1-20, 1-21).

- **Track layers:** Lets you combine takes and try alternate versions non-destructively.
- **Channel mapping:** Changes clip and track channel formats, with "adaptive" tracks supporting up to 36 channels.
- **Timeline index and keyboard shortcuts:** Index panel for clips, tracks, and markers; customizable shortcuts.
- **Sync scrollers:** Compare video frames and waveforms to align sound with picture.

**Mixing and Processing**
- **Professional mixer:** Channel strips with faders, panners, "6 effects slots for adding plug-ins," dynamics, and a 6-band parametric EQ.
- **Buses and FlexBus:** Multi-purpose busses, "up to 36 channels wide," with extensive routing.
- **Mix tools:** Gain changes across selections, plugin management, and track/bus control.
- **EQ and dynamics:** A 6-band parametric EQ and a dynamics window with "an expander/gate, compressor and limiter."
- **Automatic ducking:** The track FX ducker "uses the signal from one or more dialogue tracks" to lower a target track.
- **Automation:** "Automation tools let you record changes to virtually any control setting or effect over time."
- **Bouncing:** Renders processor-heavy clips, consolidates tracks, or creates finished audio files.
- **External processing:** Sends clips to external apps such as "Izotope RX."

**Clean-Up and Repair**
- **Fairlight FX:** "over 25 Fairlight FX plugins," including a de-esser, de-hummer, and noise reduction.
- **Noise reduction:** "automatically detects noise in a selection," or you can teach it with a "learn" function.
- **Third-party plugins:** VST and Audio Unit plugins are supported.

**Recording, Dialogue, and Sound Effects**
- **VO and multitrack recording:** Records from a simple voice-over to a full orchestra, with multiple takes stored as layers.
- **Professional ADR:** Automatic dialogue replacement with cues, prompts, and take ratings.
- **Sound effect libraries:** Audition and sync effects from external libraries within the Fairlight page.
- **Foley:** Adds foley through the sound library, ADR cues, or the Studio-only "foley sampler plug-in."

**Monitoring, Formats, and Delivery**
- **Loudness monitoring:** "Loudness meters located at the right side of the monitoring panel," with selectable metering standards, a live loudness graph, and offline "analyze audio level" analysis.

- **Delivery:** Outputs range "from mono and stereo to immersive 5.1, 7.1, 22.2 and even the latest 3D audio formats."
- **Scale:** "up to 2,000 tracks, complete with realtime effects," powered by Fairlight Audio Core.

**Hardware and Collaboration**
- **Consoles and I/O:** Desktop and modular studio consoles, plus the Audio Accelerator, MADI Upgrade, and Audio Interface.
- **Collaboration:** Multi-user project work, described as "real time project collaboration."

**Not found on this page:** Voice Isolation, Dialogue Leveler, Dialogue Processor, multiband compressor, Music Remixer, Audio Assistant, IntelliTrack, AI Dialogue Matcher, Voice Convert, and stems export. The page mentions no AI audio features, and its only AI reference (the DaVinci Neural Engine) relates to video tasks such as facial recognition.

content.content:
Fairlight
DaVinci Resolve 20 includes the following new Fairlight features and improvements.
AI IntelliCut (Studio Version Only)
AI Intellicut offers the following group of AI-driven functions.
AI Remove Silence
To increase efficiency in your workflow, this feature offers a quick, non-destructive way to remove
silent sections from your timeline clips.
Audio clip with silence indicators
     To remove silences from a timeline clip:
     1    Using the Range tool, select a clip or collection of clips on a track.
     2    Right-click the selection and choose Remove Silence in the contextual menu.
     3    The appearance of the selected audio will change to include vertical red stripes showing
          you the position and duration of the resulting silences based on the current parameter
          in the Remove Silence dialog.
          Remove Silence dialog
                                                                          DaVinci Resolve 20   Fairlight   90
 Remove Silence Parameters
    Threshold: This determines the maximum signal level of your audio (in dB) that will be
    recognized as silence. Audio signals below the threshold value will be treated as silence
    and removed. Higher threshold values result in more audio being removed.
    Pre Head: Sets the amount of silence or pre-roll before each audible section.
    Post Tail: Sets the duration of silence or post-roll after each audible section.
    Minimum to Strip: This parameter determines the minimum amount of silence
    (in milliseconds) to be stripped from selected timeline clips.
    Higher values leave more silent sections in the audio. Lower values will result in
    more strips, but you may find that some of the remaining audio sounds “chopped up”
    because it abruptly cuts off.
    Fade Head and Tail: When this checkbox is filled, fades are applied to the beginning and
    end of each remaining clip based on the Pre Head and Post Tail values.
AI Checkerboard to New Tracks
This feature is useful in situations where, for example, multiple actors are recorded with a boom
mic on a single track, and you would ideally like each voice on a separate track to make mixing
your project a lot easier.
To split speakers to new tracks:
1     Right-click the timeline clip and choose AI Tools > Checkerboard to New Tracks in the
      contextual menu.
      Ai Tools contextual menu
2     When the Transcribing Audio dialog opens, Fairlight will use AI to analyze the audio and
      identify each voice.
                                                                          DaVinci Resolve 20   Fairlight   91
 3   A new track is created for each speaker, containing their new clips. The source track will be
    muted, leaving the original timeline clip intact.
    New track timeline clips for each speaker
AI Create ADR Cues
To enhance your ADR workflow, this AI feature analyzes and transcribes a selection of timeline
clips on a track and generates individual ADR cues.
    NOTE: The dialogue must be spoken in one of the supported languages listed in the
    Project Settings under Subtitles and Transcriptions > Language. For more information
    about audio layering, see Subtitles and Transcription in Chapter 6, “Project Settings,”
    in the DaVinci Resolve Reference Manual.
Create ADR Cues offers the following output options which are explained below:
                          Timeline clip contextual menu for creating ADR cues
Create ADR Cues
Right-clicking a selection of timeline clips on a track and choosing AI Tools > Create ADR Cues
from the contextual menu opens the Transcribing Audio dialog, showing the progress of the
analysis and transcription. Once the dialog closes, the transcribed cues are added to the List
page in the ADR panel, along with their Cue ID, Time In/Out, and Durations.
New ADR cues
                                                                            DaVinci Resolve 20   Fairlight   92
 Create ADR Cues with Speakers
Right-clicking the timeline clip selection and selecting AI Tools > Create ADR Cues with Speakers
in the contextual menu adds the transcribed cues to the List page as described above, along
with the Speaker name in the Character column.
New ADR cues with speaker names added to the Character column
AI Dialogue Matcher
AI Dialogue Matcher is helpful when you need to match the ambient quality of one timeline
clip to another. For example, in a dialogue replacement scenario, you may need to make the
newly recorded dialogue sound like it was recorded in the same room as the rest of the on-
location dialog.
In this situation, AI Dialogue Matcher helps you apply the room characteristics of the original on-
location audio to the newly recorded dialogue.
    Timeline clip Dialog Matcher contextual menu
    To apply AI Dialogue Matcher:
    1   Right-click the timeline clip you want to match and choose AI Tools >
        Dialogue Matcher > Capture Dialogue Profile from the contextual menu.
    2   When the audio has been analyzed, right-click the timeline regions you want to
        apply the profile to and choose AI Tools > Dialogue Matcher > Apply Dialogue
        Profile from the contextual menu.
    Once the dialogue profile is applied, you will see a checkmark next to the Enabled
    option in the Dialogue Matcher contextual menu. Clicking this checkmark toggles the
    dialogue profile on and off. Selecting Remove Profile removes the profile from the
    clip entirely.
                                                                       DaVinci Resolve 20   Fairlight   93
 AI EQ Matcher

content.content:
AI Level Matcher
AI Level Matcher lets you match the clip volume of disparate timeline clips quickly and accurately
to each other.
    To match your clip levels with the Level Matcher:
    1   Right-click on the timeline clip you want to match and choose Clip Operations >
        Level Matching > Capture Level Profile.
        Timeline clip Level Matcher contextual menu
    2   Right-click on a timeline clip you want to adjust and choose Clip Operations
        > Level Matching > Apply Level Profile. Repeat this step for any other timeline
        clips you want to change.
AI Music Editor
The DaVinci Resolve AI Music Editor lets you lengthen or shorten music cues by creating
seamless, intelligent edits like a human music editor would do. This is achieved without using
time compression or changing the pitch.
This technology works best with beat-driven music (rock, pop, hip-hop, etc.), rather than ambient
or more free-form music.
                                                                      DaVinci Resolve 20    Fairlight   95
 Using AI Music Editor
1     Select the timeline clip of your music and go to the AI Music Editor in
      the Audio Inspector
      Ai Music Editor dialog
2     Once you have determined how long the cue needs to be, enter the length
      of time in the Target Length box and click Adjust.
      An AI Music Editor dialog will open, displaying a progress bar with the option to
      cancel the process, if needed.
      Ai Music Editor progress
      The process will try to get as close as possible to the desired length, while
      delivering four musically seamless edits you can switch between using the buttons
      in the Versions section.
    • Live Trim: Activating this function lets you dynamically trim the clip length on the
      timeline. When you have created an edit you like, you can remove the checkmark
      if you want to go back to editing (trimming) the clip normally.
TIP: If an edit ends abruptly, it can be fixed by manually creating an
appropriate fade‑out.
If the duration of an edit isn’t exactly the length you need, you can use the
Elastic Wave tool and select the general purpose (music) algorithm.
                                                                    DaVinci Resolve 20    Fairlight   96
 AI Audio Assistant (Studio Version Only)
With the new AI Audio Assistant, DaVinci Resolve can automatically organize and color code
your tracks, even out your dialogue levels, and adjust the Fairlight mixer faders to create a
professional-quality mix of your music, sound effects, and dialogue.
During this process, your dialogue will also be cleaned up, and if needed, Voice Isolation and
De-Essing will be applied. Ducking will be applied to music tracks, any required automation will
be written, and the appropriate mastering and finalizing plugins will be added and adjusted to
help achieve the correct loudness level for your chosen delivery standard.
    To use AI Audio Assistant:
    1   Open a timeline containing unmixed audio. The initial fader levels really don‘t matter
        as Audio Assistant will handle all fader adjustments during the mixing process.
    2   Ensure that you do not have differing audio elements on the same track.
    3   To begin the automatic mixing process, choose AI Tools > Audio Assistant from the
        Timeline menu, select the Delivery Standard for your mix from the dropdown menu,
        and click the Auto Mix button.
        Audio Assistant dialog
    4   The Audio Assistant dialog changes to display the progress of the mixing process
        with an option to cancel it.
        Audio Assistant dialog - Mix progress
    5   When the mixing process has concluded, you can play back the mix and,
        if needed, make further adjustments or completely undo it.
                                                                     DaVinci Resolve 20    Fairlight   97
     NOTE: If a track is in the wrong category, right-click the corresponding track
    header and choose the correct category from the Track Category section of the
    contextual menu.
Clip EQ Improvements
The Clip EQ in the Audio Inspector now support six bands, with the ability to copy and paste
setting between other Clip EQ instances.
Miscellaneous Improvements
  Improved clip gain display for multichannel clips on the timeline.
  Improved responsiveness when drawing clip waveforms for timelines with lots of clips.
  New Hairline display mode for timeline markers.
  Tracks and busses can be rearranged in the Timeline by dragging the Header color
  up or down.
  Automation Improvements:
     Automation now supports per channel mode switching.
     Trim automation now remains active through a mix pass.

The search turned up the official 18.5 guide and release notes, plus several user forum threads. The official 18.5 guide is a public beta document from April 2023, and the release notes are summarized in forum posts.

**Headline 18.5 features**
- The release was described as a massive update with new AI tools and over 150 new features, including Cut page changes, new Resolve FX, and Fusion USD support.
- Fairlight additions include track groups in Fairlight and Elastic wave time stretching now features a voice-specific option.
- Dolby Atmos work includes 9.1.6 and 5.1.4 formats, as well as support for personalized HRTF binaural rendering.

**Dialogue Leveler and Voice Isolation**
- Release notes list support for voice isolation in Studio for Linux and support for dialog leveler for Linux., along with multiple voice isolation improvements in Studio.
- Access points: Voice Isolation and Dialogue Leveler can be accessed at the clip level from the Resolve / Edit page / Inspector / Audio / Voice Isolation control, or at the track level through the Fairlight mixer's Track FX.
- Users reported problems. One thread said that previous to 18.5 I was able to turn on voice isolation under inspector and audio. Now there is just Dialogue Leveler. Another reported that rendering brings back the level jumping artifacts, so there are certainly problems with the Dialogue Leveler. These are individual user reports, not confirmed bugs, and the threads are dated.

**Fairlight FX**
- Fairlight FX Monitor Control allowing third party Rewire integration. is listed among the 18.5 additions.
- The current product page says Studio includes DaVinci Neural Engine AI voice isolation, music remixer and dialogue separator.

**Gaps:** I didn't find the full official 18.5 final release notes or a complete feature guide beyond the April 2023 beta document. Verify details against Blackmagic's current release notes before relying on them.

The search didn't return the official Resolve manual page itself. Every result is a Blackmagic Forum thread, and several point to manual pages without showing their text. Treat the details below as user-reported.

- **Manual location:** One user says the manual ships with Resolve and opens from the Help menu, and the Resolve 19 page cited for normalization is 3901 in the Rendering Media chapter. The manual is installed along with Resolve and is the first item in Resolve's Help menu.
- **BS.1770-4 preset:** A user reports the preset exposes both a true-peak target and a loudness target, with the loudness target defaulting to -23 LKFS. When you select the "BS1770-4" option, it specifically makes a new input control appear that asks you what loudness (in LKFS) you want to target. Another user, in the same thread, describes setting a -3.0 dBTP true-peak target and -14 LKFS loudness target in that preset.
- **Results conflict:** That same user reports that after normalizing, the clip measured -16.3 dBTP and -23 LUFS, which doesn't match the -3 dBTP and -14 LKFS targets they set. Another user found that it doesn't matter what you put in there, it will always use the default value. These are forum reports, not confirmed behavior.
- **EBU R128 preset:** One user says the preset fixes the true-peak limit at -1 dBTP and does not let you change it. EBU R128 specifies a True Peak Limit of -1dBTP and the Preset in the "Normalise Audio Level" window therefore uses a fixed True Peak target which is not user definable.
- **Optimise vs. Normalise (Resolve 19 Deliver page):** Normalise Loudness or Peak, conforms source levels to whichever first exceeds thresholds. Optimise Loudness and Peak, ensuring source loudness levels meet the required target range while ensuring peaks remain lower than the threshold. One user suspects the Optimise option compresses dynamics when the target isn't reached, but this isn't confirmed.
- **Relative mode (Resolve 16.1.2 manual, via a forum quote):** When Set Level is set to Relative, all selected clips are treated as if they're one clip, so that the highest peak level of all selected clips is used to define the adjustment.
- **Meters:** A forum answer says the target loudness setting affects only the Loudness meters, not normalization itself. Normalization is a separate process.

Verify the exact preset values and behavior against the manual inside your installed Resolve version, since these posts cover versions 16 through 19.

Voiceover Tool
The Cut page in DaVinci Resolve 20 has a new dedicated voiceover and teleprompter interface,
easily accessible in the Viewer by clicking on the Voiceover icon. The Voiceover tool makes it
simple to record perfectly timed scripts directly into the Cut page timeline. You can even apply
Voice Isolation and the Dialog Leveler on the fly to get great results, even with substandard
microphones and recording environments.



 Record: Starts the audio recording into the timeline.

 Stop: Stops the audio recording.

 Voice Isolation: Activates the Voice Isolation effect as you are recording, to minimize any
 background noise.

 Dialog Leveler: Activates the Dialog Leveler effect as you are recording, to keep a constant
 volume for your track.

 Stereo Fixer: Activates the Stereo Fixer effect as you are recording, to eliminate common
 channel errors involved in translating between mono and stereo sources.

Blackmagic's official DaVinci Resolve 19 New Features Guide is at documents.blackmagicdesign.com, and a forum post links to the same PDF. The search returned only excerpts, so I couldn't confirm the Dialogue Separator, Music Remixer, or Ducker sections from the guide itself.

- **IntelliTrack:** The guide describes it as a Neural Engine point tracker that is Studio-only. It is available in the Color, Fusion point, and FX trackers, and the Fusion Tracker node now defaults to it. The original point tracker remains available.
- **Dialogue Separator, Music Remixer, and Ducker:** Release notes for the 19.0 public beta list a Music Remixer FX for remixing voice, drums, bass, and other sources. They also list a Dialogue Separator FX for splitting dialogue, background, and ambience, and a Ducker track FX for automatically leveling beds under dialogue. Those are beta and forum-hosted notes, not the PDF text.
- **Ducker update in 19.1:** The 19.1 guide says the Ducker can now take several audio tracks as trigger sources, which helps when music and effects need to duck at once.
- **Other 19 highlights:** The guide also covers Dialogue Separator-adjacent speaker detection for text-based editing, UltraNR denoising, and a Fusion MultiPoly rotoscoping tool.

Version note: the original 19.0 guide is dated April 2024, and the 19.1 guide is dated November 2024. Check the 19.1 guide for the latest updates.

content.content:
IntelliTrack-Powered Audio
Panning to Video (Studio Version Only)
Totally new and unique to DaVinci Resolve, now you can automatically track people or objects
in the Fairlight viewer, generating pan automation data that matches object movement with the
precision afforded by DaVinci Resolve’s state-of-the art object tracking engine.
This can greatly accelerate creativity, saving loads of time and effort.
                                                                                           Fairlight   74
  To enable automatic tracking, ensure that the Toggle Automation switch is enabled above
  the main Fairlight tools.
                                                                                                   Fairlight   76
 Audio Effect Sidechaining
Fairlight now supports flexible sidechaining for any capable Fairlight FX and AU or VST plug-ins.
What is Sidechaining?
Sidechaining allows a track or bus signal to control the response of another plugin (often on another
audio track). This is most commonly used to control changes in a dynamics or level processor when
being fed by another source but can be used with other plugins as well for creative effect.
An example of sidechain usage would be having a dialogue bus control the amount of level
reduction or compression on background effects or music beds. Or when doing sound design,
you might have a gate whose signal input is a steady low frequency rumble, which is being
triggered to open by Foley footsteps fed into the sidechain input, so each step results in the low
frequency rumble sound being triggered on and off by the footstep.
New Track FX Plugins
Dialogue Separator, Music Remixer, and Ducker are all Track FX plugins due to their processing
buffers. They reside in dedicated insert points after Voice Isolation and Dialogue Leveler in the
TrackFX section of the Fairlight mixer.
Showing Track FX Plugins
By default, only Voice Isolation and Dialogue Leveler are shown to avoid clutter to the interface.
To make the other Track FX visible, choose the options 3 dots menu on the right of the Fairlight
mixer, make sure that Track FX section is checked on, and then choose which plugins you want
to see with “Visible Track FX” submenu at the bottom.
                        The Visible Track FX listing in Fairlight Mixer’s Option menu
Dialogue Separator
The Dialogue Separator uses DaVinci Neural Engine AI to give you individual control over the level
of dialogue, background sounds, and “ambience,” the reverberant field or ambient room sound.
                                     The Dialogue Separator controls
                                                                                             Fairlight   78
 If you have a source file that contains a great roomy sound, but there is music in the background
or crowd noises, you can rebalance so that the background sounds come down a bit or adjust
the room sound down a bit for better intelligibility.
Or you might have a situation where someone is moving closer to camera in a roomy
environment. By adjusting and automating the balances, you could make the sound roomy to
start with and get drier as it comes closer, all without affecting the background.
    NOTE: Dialogue Separator is presently mono only, so if your source is stereo, you’d
    have split into dual mono and process two mono tracks separately.
Music Remixer (Studio Version Only)
The Music Remixer is a DaVinci Neural Engine AI-based effect. This TrackFX plugin uses AI to
split music into individual basic stems: Vocals, Drums, Bass, Guitar, and “Other,” which means
“everything else.” You can use the level controls to rebalance or remix the sources, or the mute
buttons to make instant changes and bring parts in and out of your mix.
Music Remixer lets you creatively adjust a music track to suit your needs. For example, you might have
a track where you need to remove the vocal or rearrange to allow for quieter moments or a build.
                                      The Music Remixer controls
The Mute buttons let you quickly bring sections in or out for your arrangements, and you can use
automation to capture all of your changes.
Ducker
The Ducker Track FX plugin allows you to automatically lower the level of a track by using an external
source signal – this is known as “ducking.” Most commonly ducking is used to have dialogue or
VO automatically lower a music or sound effects bed, but it can be used in many creative ways.
Set up correctly, your sources can often “mix themselves” and you can create very useful results.
The Ducker uses changes in level only to do its work; the audio is not compressed or limited.
                                                                                              Fairlight   79
                                           The Ducker controls
To use the Ducker:
   Choose the target track that you want to affect (the “destination” track), and open the Ducker.
   Choose the Duck Source track or bus in the drop-down menu.
   This is the sound source you want to use to duck the level of the target track.
   If you use a bus, you can use multiple sources to trigger changes in your ducked target track.
   Play a bit of your sequence, and adjust the duck level and other controls to taste.
Ducker Controls
   Duck Amount: Controls the amount of ducking (lowering of level on the target track) in dB
    with a default of 2.7 dB. Most of the time, the amount will work best between 2 and 5 dB.
   Lookahead: Controls the amount of lookahead time in milliseconds, with a default of 15ms.
    The lookahead allows the Ducker to start to lower the destination track before the source
    track is audible. The larger the value, the more the Ducker will “pre-anticipate” the source
    track. If you want to have the Ducker start to lower the sound before a line of dialogue or
    VO begins, you can experiment with higher values, but normally the default will produce
    good results.
   Rise Time: The amount of time, in milliseconds, it takes for the Ducker to reach the amount
    of reduction specified by Duck Amount. The default is 10 ms. Most times, this value should
    be effective, but with high Duck Amount values and longer gaps in the source track’s signal,
    longer values may be useful.
   Hold: Amount of time, in milliseconds, the Ducker will hold the level reduction set by Duck
    Amount before moving to the Recovery time phase. The default is 150 ms.
   Recovery Time: Amount of time, in milliseconds, that the Ducker will take to recover from
    the Duck Amount (maximum level reduction) to no level reduction. The default is 750ms.
    Setting the Recovery Time properly can have a strong effect on whether the Ducker sounds
    “natural” or if it is distracting because level is changing too slower or quickly in response to
    the source track (e.g., dialogue). Experiment with your source material to find the best results.
Ducker Graph Display
The graph area shows a continuous representation of the level of the incoming waveform against
the action of the Ducker, shown in yellow. The yellow line mainly stays where the Duck Level puts
it; when the yellow line travels upwards, it means that the Ducker is lowering the level less, as it is
affected by gaps in the Duck Source signal and the response of the various controls.

There’s also a switch added below the graph to change between “Spectrum” and “Waterfall”
options as well as general improvements to the Waterfall display.
