Fairlight now supports flexible sidechaining for any capable Fairlight FX and AU or VST plug-ins.
What is Sidechaining?
Sidechaining allows a track or bus signal to control the response of another plugin (often on another
audio track). This is most commonly used to control changes in a dynamics or level processor when
being fed by another source but can be used with other plugins as well for creative effect.
An example of sidechain usage would be having a dialogue bus control the amount of level
reduction or compression on background effects or music beds. Or when doing sound design,
you might have a gate whose signal input is a steady low frequency rumble, which is being
triggered to open by Foley footsteps fed into the sidechain input, so each step results in the low
frequency rumble sound being triggered on and off by the footstep.

The search didn't turn up the official Fairlight FX reference manual itself, and none of the results describe the Multiband Compressor, Dialog Processor, or Vocal Channel settings.

- **Training book:** The free *Introduction to Fairlight Audio Post with DaVinci Resolve 15* covers the De-Hummer, De-Esser, and Noise Reduction plug-ins in its advanced dialogue repair lesson. In Lesson 6, you'll use advanced Fairlight FX dialogue repair tools such as the De-Hummer, De-Esser, and Noise Reduction plug-ins. It is a PDF on Blackmagic's site, and a forum user says the De-Esser step-by-step exercises start on page 217 (the Introduction to Fairlight Audio Post in DaVinci Resolve 15 training book. The PDF is available for free on the Blackmagic Design website).
- **Official product page:** Blackmagic's Fairlight page describes the clean-up plug-ins, noting de-esser to minimize annoying "s" sounds, de-hummer to remove power line hum, noise reduction plugins and more.
- **Forum mentions:** A user refers to an August 2018 "Reference Manual" that did not contain the Stereo Fixer effect (It does not come up in searches of either the August 2018 "Reference Manual" or the "Introduction to Fairlight Audio ..."). That suggests the reference manual is a separate download, but I couldn't confirm its link or whether it covers the other effects you listed.
- **Effect details:** One forum post says the De-Hummer has a Variable option along with 50Hz and 60Hz presets (the Fairlight AFX De-Hummer which provides a Variable option along with 50Hz and 60Hz presets). Another describes the De-Esser as a specialized EQ and compressor plug-in that uses a narrow frequency range to control vocal sibilance. These are user accounts, not official documentation.

For the Multiband Compressor, Dialog Processor, Vocal Channel, and Noise Reduction parameters, the Blackmagic Design support site or the Fairlight manual PDF in the DaVinci Resolve documentation would be the next place to check.

content.content:
General Improvements    8
 Optimize Audio Loudness
and Peaks in Render Settings
In the Audio Render settings tab in the Delivery page, a new Audio Normalization audio option is
available with options to:
   Normalize loudness or peak (scaling whichever first exceeds thresholds) to a standard,
   Optimize loudness and peak (ensuring that loudness meets the desired range and peaks
    remain lower than threshold),
   Use the bus or track audio as-is.

This is enabled by checking on “Normalize Audio” and then choosing the appropriate
sub-options.




                                        The Audio Normalization settings


Fairlight FX Improvements
Track FX on Stereo Linked Groups
Track effects can now be applied to stereo-linked groups (stereo-linked tracks).
Ducker – Multiple Audio Tracks as Input Sources
The Ducker now supports using multiple audio tracks as input sources, which, for example,
is useful when mixing a scene where three characters are having a conversation next to a
noisy freeway.
In this instance, with only one input source (Dialogue 1), the Ducker would only be effective when
the first character speaks. This new feature lets you use the audio tracks for other characters
(Dialogue 2 and Dialogue 3) as input sources for attenuating the traffic noise.

**What it does:** Studio Sound is an AI effect that improves recorded voice audio. It "enhances spoken voice by reducing background noise, echo, and other distractions." It works on recorded audio, not AI-generated text-to-speech.

**Internet:** The docs say it "requires an internet connection," but they don't explicitly describe the processing as cloud-based.

**Intensity slider:** Use it to "control how much enhancement is applied to the file." Lowering it helps if a very noisy recording makes the waveform go flat or silent.

**Where it applies:**
- **Source file:** Once enabled, it is applied at the file level, so it affects every instance of that file in your project.
- **Script layer:** Select the layer, then toggle Studio Sound on in the Properties panel's Audio Effects section.
- **Sequence:** In the Sequence Editor, select the track and enable it in the Properties panel.
- **Part of a file:** Duplicate the section into a new composition, flatten it, apply Studio Sound to the new file, and replace the original section.

**Recording option:** Yes. You can "enable Studio Sound while recording in the main editor" or use it with the Screen Recorder.

content.content:
Ducking follows the **clip extent on the layer, not the speech itself**. The effect is "based on clip presence—not audio content or transcription," so "even background noise or breathing will keep other layers lowered as long as the clip exists on the timeline." Other layers return to full volume only where the track is empty or covered by a gap clip.

**Controls:**
- **Enable:** Select the layer, open the Properties panel, click **+** under Audio Effects, then choose Dynamics > Lower audio of other layers.
- **Amount:** Use the Effect settings icon next to the toggle. Lower percentages make other layers quieter, so the ducking is stronger.
- **Multiple tracks:** Enabling it on several tracks doesn't make them reduce each other, only other layers. If the tracks use different amounts, Descript applies the strongest reduction.

**Limitations:** It applies to the whole layer and can't be limited to individual clips. It isn't available in the Sequence Editor, so use the composition timeline instead.

content.content:
**Edit for Clarity:** An AI tool that cuts rambling, repeated, and off-topic material, with an optional AI-speech reword. It's in the "Sound Good" tools.

**Studio Sound:** AI voice enhancement that lowers background noise and echo, with adjustable intensity. It is not a recording studio.

**Regenerate:** An AI feature that re-synthesizes a speaker's recorded audio, and optionally their video, to fix pronunciation, change words, heal jump cuts, or smooth pacing. Changing words requires an authorized custom AI Speaker and works only in English. It doesn't involve re-recording.

**AI voice / Overdub / voice clone:**
- **AI voice (AI Speaker):** A synthetic voice, either stock or custom, that generates speech from script text.
- **Overdub:** This term has three meanings. Its legacy meaning, fixing or changing recorded words, is now **Regenerate**. Its older meaning of generating speech from typed text in a cloned voice is now **AI Speakers / text-to-speech**. Its traditional audio meaning of layering a new recording over existing audio is done by adding an audio layer or recording into the timeline.
- **Voice clone:** The content doesn't define this term. The closest match is a custom AI Speaker.

**Remove Retakes:** An AI tool that finds re-recorded phrases and marks the earlier takes as ignored text for removal.

**Shorten Word Gaps:** Use this feature to reduce pauses and silence between words. It's found under the word gap term.

**Filler words:** Words like "um," "uh," "like," and "you know." You can detect and remove them with Remove Filler Words.

**Multitrack sequence:** A sequence is a container that keeps grouped tracks in sync, such as separate video and audio from one recording. It is sometimes called a "multi-track sequence." It is not a composition.

**Lower other audio:** The content doesn't define this term.

**Other audio-related terms:**
- **Word boundary:** The start and end points that align the transcript with the media. You can adjust them manually.
- **Wordbar:** The timeline area showing the words from the script's audio, where you adjust word boundaries and gaps.
- **Dub / Dub speech:** Generates a spoken translated voiceover. It pairs with lip sync to match mouth movement.
- **Ignore:** Strikes through text to remove its media from playback without deleting it.

The search turned up Telestream's ScreenFlow help pages and guides, but no single current page that covers all of these options together.

- **Ducking:** In the Audio Properties panel, checking the Ducking option lowers the volume of overlapping audio, with a slider for the reduction percentage. Checking it adjusts volume levels on overlapping audio clips, and all overlapping audio is muted to draw attention to the audio in this clip.
- **Smooth Volume Levels:** This is an audio-properties option, not a filter. It normalizes and smooths volume peaks while raising quieter clips for a more consistent volume. The ScreenFlow 3.0 guide describes it as combining limiting, compression and more.
- **Remove Background Noise:** This is a filter. It reduces the volume of incidental background noise, with a sensitivity slider.
- **Adding filters (ScreenFlow 10 guide):** Select the clip, open the Audio tab, click the (+) next to Audio Filters, and search by name. In the Audio tab, you can enter a filter name into the Search field and press Enter.
- **Normalize:** I found no separate named normalize filter in these results. The index lists "normalize," but the search didn't show what it refers to.

The Audio Properties page is from an older online help version, so the exact menu labels may differ in current releases. The current user guide PDF (version 10) is the best place to confirm them.

The search turned up consistent answers from TechSmith's own documentation.

- **What it does:** Emphasize is applied to a clip, such as narration, and lowers the volume of every other audio track on the timeline while that clip plays. Apply the Emphasize audio effect to voice narration clips to automatically decrease the volume of all other audio tracks.
- **Strength:** The Emphasis slider sets how much the other tracks drop. At the maximum setting, the other tracks are muted for the length of the clip (drag the Emphasis slider to change the volume for all other audio tracks on the timeline. 100% mutes the audio of the other tracks for the duration of the applied clip.).
- **Transition timing:** Ramp Position controls where the volume change happens relative to the clip. The options are Outside, Span, and Inside, and a value in seconds sets the Ramp In and Ramp Out durations (Select Ramp Position to set where the volume transition starts and ends on the timeline.).
- **How to apply it:** Open the Audio Effects tab and drag Emphasize onto the clip. Then open Properties and the Audio Properties subtab to adjust it (Click the Audio Effects tab. Drag the Emphasize effect onto any clip on the timeline that includes your narration or microphone recording.).
- **Version note:** Behavior changed across releases. One Mac version note says the Emphasize audio effect is now automatically applied to microphone recordings. A later one says automatic adding of the Emphasize effect to audio was removed in 2023.3.15. Check your version if you expect it to be on automatically.

The sources are TechSmith's Camtasia help and tutorial pages, and the Mac version history. I did not find any reports of the effect failing to work as described.

content.content:
The page covers these audio editing features in Camtasia Editor:

- **Audio points:** You can add points to change volume in part of a clip. "Double-click on the audio bar to add points." Points can be moved up, down, or sideways, and deleted.
- **Volume:** Clip level can be set with the Gain slider in the Audio subtab or by dragging the audio bar. Project-wide level uses a master gain slider. The page notes that "Adjust the audio level for the whole project" is done from the volume indicator below the Properties button.
- **Fades:** Fades use three audio points, or the Fade In/Fade Out effects. "To create a fade, add three audio points to the audio bar."
- **Separate audio and video:** You can split system audio from a screen recording with "Separate Video and Audio."
- **Muting:** The page doesn't mention a mute control. It describes silencing a selected section instead, using "Silence Audio."
- **Waveform editing:** The only waveform option is "Mirror waveform," which is available on Windows only.
- **Export:** You can use "Export Audio Only" to save M4A, WAV, or MP3 (MP3 is Windows only).
- **Other options:** "Mix to Mono" puts audio in both channels.

The page does not mention keyframes, normalization, or loudness settings on export.

content.content:
The page describes six audio effects. Volume Leveling, Compressor, EQ, AI noise removal, Normalize, Remove reverb, and Enhance voice are not on the page. The closest match to Volume Leveling is the Volume variation setting in Audio Compression.

**Audio Compression**
- Controls: a **Volume variation** dropdown, or manual **Ratio**, **Threshold**, and **Gain** settings.
- Purpose: "Helps even out audio levels."
- Platform notes: none stated.

**Clip Speed**
- Controls: drag the effect handles on the timeline, or use **Properties** to set **Speed** or **Duration**. A higher speed makes playback faster, and a lower speed makes it slower.
- Purpose: "Change audio and video clip to play back faster or slower."
- Platform notes: none stated.

**Emphasize**
- Controls: an **Emphasis** slider (at 100%, other tracks are muted for the clip's duration), **Ramp Position** (Outside, Span, or Inside), and **Ramp In** and **Ramp Out** durations in seconds.
- Purpose: "Emphasizes the audio for the applied media by decreasing the volume of all other audio tracks."
- Platform notes: none stated.

**Fade In / Fade Out**
- Controls: applied automatically to the start or end of a clip. Drag the audio points to adjust.
- Purpose: "Creates smooth transition in to or out of audio."
- Platform notes: none stated.

**Pitch (Mac Only)**
- Controls: **Pitch**, **Ease In**, and **Ease Out**.
- Purpose: "Adjust frequency of sound waves to change voice sound."
- Platform notes: the page labels this effect Mac only.

**Noise Removal**
- Controls: an **Analyze** button for automated removal, or manual **Sensitivity** plus **Reduction** (Mac) or **Amount** (Windows).
- Purpose: "Helps reduce background noise."
- Platform notes: "Click **Analyze** to automate noise removal process (Windows only)." The manual control's name differs by platform.

                Volume
                The slider, and accompanying text field, provide the volume adjustment for the Audio
                Mixer. The volume is set to 100% by default, but can be reset above or below this value.
                Mute Audio
                Check to mute all audio output from the mixer.

                Check to activate ducking. This lowers the audio levels for background audio whenever

                entering a value and pressing Enter. ScreenFlow updates the slider accordingly.

                  Displays the audio output of the mixer using a stereo meter bar.

                  The effect pane contains the following:
                  Effect
                  Check to activate effects. Select an effect from the pull-down menu.
                  Amount
                  Move the slider to adjust the amount of effect you want in your audio output. You can

                  Check Remove Background Noise to remove or lower the background noise in your

                  “x” icon (to the right of each filter name)

                  The Audio Mixer
                  You can mix, pan, and solo all of your audio channels using the controls in the audio
                  mixer. The Audio Mix panel is closed by default, but you can open it by clicking on the
                  triangle next to Audio Mix. ScreenFlow displays each individual input channel. The
                  Audio Mix dialog contains the following:
                  Gear icon
                  Click to open the options menu where you can select Rest to defaults or Set Mix to Mono.
                                                                                       ScreenFlow User Guide
                                                                                  Windows in ScreenFlow        115
                                                                                  The Properties Window
                Channel Number
                Each individual audio channel has a number of controls. On the far left is the channel
                number string; this is simply the index of the channel.
                Audio Meter
                Next to the number is an audio meter showing the RMS power, peak and peak hold of
                audio in that channel. The meter is dB based and has a scale from -72 to +6. If the peak
                goes above 0dB, the meter will be tinted red to let the user know clipping is occurring.
                Once the peak hold decays below 0dB, the meter resumes its normal look. The lighter
                green value is the RMS power, which provides a general indication of the current
                loudness of the channel. The darker green color is the current peak dB value and the
                white line is the current peak hold value.
                Solo Buttons
                To the right of the audio meter is the 'S' or Solo button. This mutes all other channels in
                the mix during preview. Selecting the solo button for one channel automatically
                deselects the solo buttons for all other channels. To monitor more than one channel,
                press the command key while clicking solo buttons on desired channels. Clicking an
                already-selected Solo button without holding down the command key deactivates solo
                track preview. When the Solo button is selected for one channel, the audio meters for
                all other channels are disabled, and turn a gray shade.
                Note: The Solo button state is not saved to the document.
                Pan Controls
                The control next to the Solo button is the pan button. The pan function in the audio
                mixer determines how much of the channel is mixed to the left & right channels of the
                final mix. When the pan control is in the middle (0%), the input channel is mixed equally
                to both left & right output channels. When the pan is at -100% (all the way to the left),
                the input channel is being mixed only to the left output channel. If it is 100% (all the
                way to the right), the input channel is being mixed only to the right output channel. If
                the pan is set to -50%, 100% of input channel will be sent to the left channel, which 50%
                will be sent to the right. This is particularly useful when the ScreenFlow is using two
                microphones: one can slightly favor each channel. When a stereo media is imported
                into ScreenFlow, its audio mix will be setup by default to have the left input channel at
                -100% pan, and the right input channel at 100% pan.
                Note: This setup emulates how earlier versions of ScreenFlow behave: the left input
                channel is sent to the left output channel, and the right input channel is sent to the
                right output channel. Please be aware that the 'Mix to Mono' feature has been
                removed: this functionality can now be achieved with audio mixer's pan feature.
                Slider
                The slider and accompanying text field provide the volume adjustment for the input
                channel. The volume is 100% by default, but can be boosted beyond or below this
                value.

Adobe's documentation covers the Audio Gain dialog's normalization options in Premiere Pro. The main points:

- **Opening the dialog:** Adobe's help page says Clip > Audio Options > Audio Gain (shortcut G) opens it, and it calculates the selected clips' peak amplitude, shown in the Peak Amplitude field. Choose Clip > Audio Options > Audio Gain or keyboard shortcut G. The Audio Gain dialog box opens. Premiere Pro automatically calculates the peak amplitude of the selected clips.
- **Manual adjustment:** You can either set an absolute gain or add a dB offset. Adobe's page describes "Set Gain to" (default 0.0 dB) and "Adjust Gain by" (also default 0.0 dB), with the two fields kept in sync. Entering a value other than zero in this field automatically updates the Set Gain To dB value to reflect the actual gain value applied to the clip.
- **Normalize Max Peak to:** This sets the loudest point of the selected clips to a chosen level below 0 dB. It option adjusts the maximum peak amplitude in the selected clips to the user-specified value.
- **Normalize All Peaks to:** This applies the same kind of target to the peak of each selected clip individually. This normalization option adjusts the peak amplitude in the selected clips to the user-specified value.
- **Common target:** An Adobe tutorial suggests -18 dB as a generally good starting point for matching clip levels in a sequence, and notes that the level of all the selected clips is adjusted automatically to match the volume you chose.
- **Dialogue alternative:** For dialogue, Adobe suggests the Essential Sound panel instead. Both options work well: Audio Gain adjustment (useful for music clips), and the Essential Sound panel (useful for dialogue).

Caveats: Peak normalization sets the loudest sample, not perceived loudness, so clips with different dynamics can still sound uneven. Adobe also notes that if the level of an audio clip was set too low when it was digitized, increasing the gain or volume amplifies noise. The "Normalize Dialog" option mentioned in Premiere Elements is a different feature and does not appear in these Premiere Pro results.

The search turned up Adobe's official help pages on the round trip, the Essential Sound panel, and AI auto-tagging.

- **Sending a sequence:** Adobe's sequence guide says a Premiere sequence sent to Audition keeps its keyframes, effects, Essential Sound settings, markers, and metadata (Sending a sequence to Audition transfers the full fidelity of your composition, keeping keyframes, effects, Essential Sound settings, markers, and metadata intact.). The Edit in Adobe Audition dialog also controls audio handles and render settings.
- **Sending a single clip:** The clip is rendered to a new Wave file that opens in Audition (the clip is rendered and replaced into a new Wave file which directly opens in Audition.). Changes saved in Audition show up in the Premiere timeline. Each new send replaces the previous rendered file. The command is not available for dynamic link clips.
- **Essential Sound round trip:** Audition uses the same four audio types, Dialogue, Music, SFX, and Ambience (Audition allows you to classify your audio clips as Dialogue, Music, SFX, or Ambience.).
- **AI auto-tagging:** Premiere's Audio Category Tagging applies those four types automatically. To use it, you select one or more clips in the timeline and choose Auto Tag in the Essential Sound panel, which then adds category badges to each clip (Select one or multiple audio files in the timeline and select Auto Tag in the Essential Sound panel. Once auto-tagging is complete, interactive Essential Sound badges will be shown on each audio clip.).

I didn't find a source that explicitly describes auto-tagging carrying through the Premiere-to-Audition round trip, so that part is unconfirmed. The auto-tag page is also about 689 days old, so the current UI may differ.

Premiere Pro's split edits (J-cuts and L-cuts) rely on unlinking clips so audio and video can be trimmed separately.

- **Unlinking:** Right-click a clip and choose Unlink, which makes the audio and video behave independently. Once unlinked, you can use the video and audio as though they were not linked, though Premiere Pro still tracks the link. Newer versions list this under Clip > Unlink. To unlink a linked clip, select the clip and then select Clip > Unlink.
- **Alternative toggle:** Disabling Linked Selection with its icon in the Timeline panel lets you select audio or video independently.
- **Quick, temporary override:** Holding Alt (Windows) or Option (macOS) while trimming or dragging temporarily unlinks the clips. Alt-dragging or Option-dragging a clip's audio or video is a common way to adjust a split edit quickly, and it is much faster than unlinking.
- **Making the cut:** After unlinking, select the Rolling Edit tool and drag the audio edit point between two clips. If nothing happens, position the pointer over the visible audio edit point rather than over an applied audio transition.
- **Setting split points at source:** In the Source Monitor, you can set separate in and out points for video and audio using Mark Split. After selecting a portion of the clip, right-click and choose Mark Split, then pick Video In, Video Out, Audio In, or Audio Out.
- **Razor tool:** Alt-click (Windows) or Option-click (macOS) with the Razor tool splits only the audio or video portion of linked clips.
- **J-cut vs. L-cut:** A J-cut lets the next scene's audio start before its picture changes, which builds anticipation. An L-cut lets the previous scene's audio carry over onto the next scene's picture, which keeps the transition smooth. Adobe's guide also says to make a J cut, drag the preceding clip so the next clip's audio overlaps the footage; for an L cut, stretch the next clip's video over the preceding clip's audio track.

Sources: Adobe's Premiere Pro help pages on editing audio in the timeline, creating J and L cuts, linking clips, trim mode, and cutting clips. Some pages are dated, and the menu names may differ slightly between versions.

content.content:
[Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

## The ruler and the playhead

The ruler's ticks adjust to the zoom, from single frames up to minutes.
Labels drop the hours when the timeline is under an hour long. The playhead
is the coral line with a triangle head on the ruler.

- **Click the ruler** to move the playhead there, and **drag** along it to
  scrub. Playback stops while you scrub. The scrub snaps like any other drag
  (see [Snapping](#snapping)).
- The timeline scrolls itself to keep the playhead in view: when the playhead
  leaves the visible part, during playback or after a jump, the view moves
  so the playhead sits about a third of the way in.
- A click in a lane doesn't move the playhead. It starts a marquee selection
  (see [Selecting clips](#selecting-clips)).
68:Hold ⌥ while you drag a media clip's **end** edge to stretch it instead. The clip's speed changes so that the same content fills the new length (undo name "Rate Stretch"). ⌥ on the start edge does an ordinary trim. If a stretch would take the clip above the speed where its sound is dropped, the app asks first. Speeds and their limits are covered in [Speed](speed.md).
156:| Audio | Everything: volume, pan, fades, effects | — |
160:The target keeps its place, length, speed, animation actions, transition, name, label, and which halves (picture and sound) are switched on. If nothing would change, it beeps.
164:## Splitting picture from sound
166:**Clip ▸ Detach Audio** (⌥⌘D) switches off each selected clip's sound and adds an audio-only copy of it on the track below, at the same time, with the same footage and speed. If the clip is on the back track, a new track is added behind it. Undo name: "Detach Audio".
168:Each clip that can't be detached is refused with a reason: "clip … has no audio to detach: it is not a media clip", "…: media … has no audio track", or "…: its audio is switched off".
170:A clip's picture and sound can each be switched on or off. The app's only control for this is Detach Audio. Agents can set either half directly.
172:*Agents:* `detach_audio` takes `clip`. `set_enabled` takes `clip` and `video` and/or `audio` (true or false). Leave one out to keep its value.
251:- **A menu command or key** is one step, even when it changes many clips. Examples: Ripple Delete over a range, Un-nest of several nests, Detach Audio on a selection, a Remove Silences pass.
290:| ⌥⌘D | Detach Audio |
107:- move, trim, split, slip, roll, rate-stretch, ripple-delete, lift, insert time and close gaps; detach audio
110:- change how a clip looks and sounds, including transitions, actions and zooms; rename a clip, hide or mute it, and paste attributes
112:- find silences and filler words, normalize loudness and synchronize audio
123:**Cutting words.** Ask it to take out filler words and it finds them and cuts them in one step, but only in media that already have a cloud transcript made with filler words (by **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…**). The assistant can't upload audio to make one, so in other media it cuts nothing (the search reports which media have no such transcript). Ask it to remove a false start and it reads the clip's words and their times (from the media's cached transcript, or from this Mac's own speech recogniser, never the network), says which words it will cut, then cuts them as one undo step. It removes a false start only when you ask, because deciding what was a false start is a judgement call. See [Clean-up tools](cleanup-tools.md).
133:| `transcribe` with the cloud engine (AssemblyAI) | Audio leaves the machine only when you choose it, with the price in front of you. | **File ▸ Generate Captions…** |
134:| `transcribe_for_fillers` | The same: it uploads audio to the cloud. | **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…** |
228:Frame Job doesn't send any of this anywhere else. Audio never goes to the cloud transcriber from the assistant (see [Tools it will not call](#tools-it-will-not-call)). The assistant asks before it exports a movie or captions, saves the project, or consolidates media; other tools can still write files without asking (a rendered frame's PNG, and graphics modules, fonts and assets in the project's package). Once a day at most, the helper downloads LiteLLM's public price table from GitHub. That request carries no key and no project data.
236:- It can't record the screen, close its window's project, or send audio to the cloud transcriber.

content.content:
**Abstract**

> "Sets the engine to operate in manual rendering mode with the render format and maximum frame count you specify."

**Platforms**

- iOS 11.0+
- iPadOS 11.0+
- Mac Catalyst 13.1+
- macOS 10.13+
- tvOS 11.0+
- visionOS 1.0+
- watchOS 4.0+

**Discussion**

> "Use this method to configure the engine to render in response to requests from the client. You must stop the engine before calling this method. The render format must be a PCM format and match the format of the rendering buffer."

> "The source nodes can supply the input data in manual rendering mode. For more information, see AVAudioPlayerNode and AVAudioInputNode."

The page covers the method `enableManualRenderingMode(_:format:maximumFrameCount:)`, which is the setup step for manual rendering. The "offline" mode is referenced on the related `renderOffline(_:to:)` page, whose abstract says it "Makes a render call to the engine operating in the offline manual rendering mode."

**Illustrative usage (not from the page)**

```swift
let engine = AVAudioEngine()
// ... attach and connect nodes, then stop the engine first ...
engine.stop()

let format = AVAudioFormat(standardFormatWithSampleRate: 44_100, channels: 2)!
do {
    try engine.enableManualRenderingMode(.offline, format: format, maximumFrameCount: 4096)
    try engine.start()
} catch {
    print("Failed to enable manual rendering: \(error)")
}
```

The search didn't turn up an Apple sample project that combines AudioTapProcessor, MTAudioProcessingTap, and a bandpass audio unit. It did surface related material:

- **Tap attachment:** Apple's QA1783 says a tap is linked to a track through the `audioTapProcessor` property of `AVMutableAudioMixInputParameters` (developer.apple.com/library/archive/qa/qa1783/_index.html).
- **Pre- vs. post-effects:** The same Q&A explains the creation flags that decide whether the tap runs before or after the mix's effects. A developer forum thread (developer.apple.com/forums/thread/90879) reports that post-effects taps didn't reflect volume ramps. It includes a full Swift code sample with a `process` callback.
- **Bandpass unit:** Apple's legacy "System-Supplied Audio Units" page lists AUBandpass as a single-band bandpass filter (developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/MusicAudio/Conceptual/CoreAudioOverview/SystemAudioUnits/SystemAudioUnits.html). That page covers OS X 10.5, so it's dated.
- **HLS limitation:** A forum thread (developer.apple.com/forums/thread/45966) says MTAudioProcessingTap wasn't available for HTTP Live Streaming. Apple's newer HLS material (developer.apple.com/streaming/Whats-new-HLS.pdf) says taps can now process HLS output, except FairPlay-protected audio, and that the tap is set up through `audioTapProcessor` with `AVAudioMixInputParametersTrackMixID`.
- **iOS 17 issue:** A forum thread (developer.apple.com/forums/thread/737949) reports crackling with two AVPlayers that each use a tap-equipped audio mix, while AVQueuePlayer worked.

To build a bandpass filter, you would likely host an AUBandpass (or AVAudioUnitEQ) inside your tap's process callback, or run it through AVAudioEngine. I didn't find an official sample for that exact setup, so check Apple's sample code library directly.

"""Measure a voice recording for the audio survey: level distribution, SNR,
band energies, hum, sibilance, short-term loudness spread. Reads via ffmpeg."""
import subprocess
import sys

import numpy as np

path = sys.argv[1]
sr = 48000
raw = subprocess.run(
    ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(sr), "-f", "f32le", "-"],
    check=True, capture_output=True,
).stdout
x = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).astype(np.float64)
print(f"samples {len(x)}  duration {len(x)/sr:.2f} s")


def db(v):
    return 20 * np.log10(max(v, 1e-12))


print(f"sample peak {db(np.max(np.abs(x))):.1f} dBFS, rms {db(np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2))):.1f} dBFS")

# 50 ms window RMS distribution
w = int(0.05 * sr)
n = len(x) // w
frames = x[: n * w].reshape(n, w)
rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(frames**2, axis=1))
rdb = np.array([db(r) for r in rms])
for p in (5, 10, 20, 50, 80, 90, 95, 99):
    print(f"50ms RMS p{p:02d}: {np.percentile(rdb, p):6.1f} dBFS")
noise = np.percentile(rdb, 10)
speech = np.percentile(rdb, 90)
print(f"estimated SNR (p90 - p10): {speech - noise:.1f} dB")
print(f"fraction of windows within 6 dB of the floor: {np.mean(rdb < noise + 6):.2f}")

# spectrum: whole file and quiet-only windows
def band_energy(sig, lo, hi):
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(sig * np.hanning(len(sig)))) ** 2
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(sig), 1 / sr)
    return spec, f


nfft = 8192
hop = 4096
segs = []
quiet_segs = []
for i in range(0, len(x) - nfft, hop):
    s = x[i : i + nfft]
    p = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(s * np.hanning(nfft))) ** 2
    segs.append(p)
    if db(np.sqrt(np.mean(s**2))) < noise + 3:
        quiet_segs.append(p)
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(nfft, 1 / sr)
P = np.mean(segs, axis=0)
Q = np.mean(quiet_segs, axis=0) if quiet_segs else None
tot = P.sum()


def frac(spec, lo, hi):
    m = (f >= lo) & (f < hi)
    return 10 * np.log10(spec[m].sum() / spec.sum())


bands = [(0, 40), (40, 80), (80, 160), (160, 300), (300, 1000), (1000, 4000), (4000, 5000), (5000, 9000), (9000, 16000), (16000, 24000)]
print("band share of energy (whole file):")
for lo, hi in bands:
    print(f"  {lo:5d}-{hi:5d} Hz: {frac(P, lo, hi):6.1f} dB")
if Q is not None:
    print(f"quiet windows: {len(quiet_segs)} of {len(segs)}; band share of energy in quiet windows:")
    for lo, hi in bands:
        print(f"  {lo:5d}-{hi:5d} Hz: {frac(Q, lo, hi):6.1f} dB")

# hum: peak at 50/60 Hz and harmonics vs neighbouring bins, in quiet windows
spec = Q if Q is not None else P
for base in (50, 60):
    out = []
    for h in range(1, 6):
        fc = base * h
        k = np.argmin(np.abs(f - fc))
        neigh = np.r_[spec[max(k - 12, 0) : k - 3], spec[k + 4 : k + 13]]
        out.append(10 * np.log10(spec[k - 1 : k + 2].max() / np.median(neigh)))
    print(f"hum {base} Hz harmonics 1..5 peak over neighbours (dB): " + ", ".join(f"{v:.1f}" for v in out))

# sibilance: per-window ratio of 5-9 kHz to 300-4000 Hz energy, on loud windows
ratios = []
for i in range(0, len(x) - 2048, 1024):
    s = x[i : i + 2048]
    if db(np.sqrt(np.mean(s**2))) < speech - 20:
        continue
    p = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(s * np.hanning(2048))) ** 2
    ff = np.fft.rfftfreq(2048, 1 / sr)
    hi = p[(ff >= 5000) & (ff < 9000)].sum()
    mid = p[(ff >= 300) & (ff < 4000)].sum()
    ratios.append(10 * np.log10(hi / mid))
ratios = np.array(ratios)
print(f"sibilance ratio 5-9k vs 0.3-4k on active windows: p50 {np.percentile(ratios,50):.1f} dB, p95 {np.percentile(ratios,95):.1f} dB, max {ratios.max():.1f} dB")

Apple's Final Cut Pro for Mac support pages cover the fade shapes you asked about, in two places.

**Fade handles in the timeline:** Control-clicking a fade handle offers Linear, S-curve, +3dB, and –3dB. Apple's pages describe Linear as a steady rate of change across the fade, and S-curve as easing in and out with the midpoint at 0 dB (Linear: Maintains a constant rate of change over the length of the fade. S-curve: Eases in and out of the fade with the midpoint at 0 dB.). Apple also notes that the shape affects how the fade sounds (Changing the fade shape changes the sound of the fade.).

**+3dB and –3dB:** The +3dB curve is the default. Apple recommends it for keeping volume natural when crossfading two clips, and it has fade-ins that rise quickly before leveling off (+3dB: Fade-ins start quickly and end slowly; fade-outs start slowly and end quickly. This is the default setting and is best for maintaining a natural volume when crossfading between two clips.). The –3dB curve reverses that pattern (–3dB: Fade-ins start slowly and end quickly; fade-outs start quickly and end slowly.).

**Crossfade transitions:** For a transition's audio crossfade, the Transition inspector's Audio Crossfade section lets you set Fade In Type and Fade Out Type separately, using the same options (In the Audio Crossfade section of the Transition inspector, click the Fade In Type pop-up menu or the Fade Out Type pop-up menu and choose a fade option). Apple's wording for the +3dB and –3dB descriptions there differs a little from the fade-handle pages.

**Applying fades:** Modify > Adjust Audio Fades > Apply Fades adds default fades to selected clips, and Remove Fades clears them. Apply Fades won't override a clip that already has a fade (If you select a clip that already has a fade, the Apply Fades command does not override it.).

I ran one search, so I didn't check whether these pages reflect the latest Final Cut Pro version. One of the cited pages is about 1,800 days old.

Adobe's help documentation covers this workflow in Premiere Pro's Text-Based Editing feature:

The sources don't clearly say which filter options exist in the newest version, so check your own build.

- **Limits:** Speaker-based removal only works on a sequence or timeline. Footage cannot be deleted from source transcriptions.

Adobe's help pages describe the three Premiere Pro audio crossfades, though they don't say much about the exact curve math.

- **Constant Gain:** The volume changes at a steady rate on both clips. Adobe notes that this can sometimes result in a noticeable dip in volume at the midpoint of the transition.
- **Constant Power:** This is the default crossfade. Adobe describes it as the audio counterpart to a video dissolve. The outgoing clip decreases audio for the first clip slowly at first and then quickly toward the end, and the incoming clip rises in the opposite pattern.
- **Exponential Fade:** Adobe's descriptions differ slightly. One says the transition fades out the first clip over a smooth logarithmic curve while fading up the second clip. Another says it sounds similar to the Constant Power transition, it's more gradual in nature.

For practical use, the Effects panel lets you set Constant Gain or Constant Power as the default transition. To customize a crossfade's rate, Adobe suggests adjusting the clip's volume keyframe graph rather than applying a transition. For a crossfade between two clips, the clips must be adjacent and on the same track, and you can drag the fade handles to shape the curve. Holding Option while dragging changes the curve or duration.

Apple's Final Cut Pro for Mac support guide covers this in its "Sync audio and video" section.

- **Automatic sync:** Select the clips in the browser, then choose Clip > Synchronize Clips (Option-Command-G). The app checks for sync points such as markers, timecode, file creation date, and audio content, then creates a new synced clip in the event you pick. Final Cut Pro analyzes the clips for sync points such as markers you've added, timecode, file creation date, and audio content.
- **Custom settings:** The Synchronization pop-up menu offers Automatic, Timecode, Content Created, Start of First Clip, and First Marker options. Timecode is the fastest and most frame-accurate method when clips have recorded timecode (It's the fastest and most frame-accurate method of syncing clips.).
- **"Use audio for synchronization":** This option is in the custom settings. It makes precision sync adjustments using audio waveforms. Apple also notes that selecting this option may result in long processing times during which Final Cut Pro is not available for editing. It also doesn't suit every recording: some audio recordings are not suited for use with this feature.
- **Combining options:** Apple suggests pairing a marker with the audio option. Using the first marker as a rough sync point, then fine-tuned with the "Use audio for synchronization" option, works well.
- **Fixing a sync:** Open the synced clip with Clip > Open Clip, then drag the connected clips left or right to slip the sync.

Source: Apple Support, "Sync audio and video in Final Cut Pro for Mac" (support.apple.com/guide/final-cut-pro). The page was about 1,579 days old when indexed, so the menu names may differ in newer versions.

Adobe's help pages describe two workflows, and the most relevant point for waveform syncing is a limitation.

- **Merge Clips** is Premiere's way to sync separately recorded audio with video. You can attach up to 16 audio channels to one video clip, and you can merge audio-only clips with each other. Select the video clip you wish to merge audio clips to. Note that you can have only one video clip in any merged clip. Sync points can be based on In points, Out points, matching timecode, or numbered clip markers. Based on the Clip Start, Based on the Clip End, Based on matching timecode, Based on clip markers are the timeline Synchronize options.

- **Synchronize in the Timeline** aligns clips you've already placed on the timeline. You can drag them into position by hand, or use Clip > Synchronize. Audio track channel: Offers option to specify one audio track to be used as the reference for syncing when you have multiple audio channels.

- **Waveform auto-sync is not supported for merged clips.** The limitations page lists auto-sync using audio waveforms, free-run timecode, time-of-day timecode, AUX timecode, or separate audio timecode is not supported. Also, once created, the merged clip cannot be re-synchronized, or adjusted. To re-snyc or adjust your clips, make a new merged clip.

- **Waveform-based syncing for multicam** is handled differently. The Create Multi-Camera Source Sequence dialog offers an Audio option: Use this option to synchronize clips based on a specific audio track. This is helpful when a consistent audio source is present in all clips (like a clapboard or voiceover).

Practical takeaway: for waveform-matched sync, use the Synchronize or multicam audio options before merging, because a merged clip can't be re-synced later. The search results don't include step-by-step instructions for the audio-waveform option itself, and the pages I found are from Adobe's help site with somewhat varying publication dates.

**Abstract**

> "A request that classifies sound using a Core ML model."

**Platforms**

- iOS 13.0+
- iPadOS 13.0+
- Mac Catalyst 13.1+
- macOS 10.15+
- tvOS 13.0+
- visionOS 1.0+
- watchOS 6.0+

**Overview (discussion)**

> "An `SNClassifySoundRequest` represents a specific sound classification model. Analyze audio data with a sound classification model by:"
>
> 1. "Creating an `SNClassifySoundRequest`, either with the Sound Analysis model, or by providing your custom Core ML model."
> 2. "Adding the sound request to an `SNAudioFileAnalyzer` or `SNAudioStreamAnalyzer` to process an audio file or stream, respectively."

**Built-in classifier: number of classes**

This page does not say how many sound classes the built-in classifier recognizes, and it does not mention speech or music as categories. The only related information is in the abstract of the linked "Classifying Live Audio Input with a Built-in Sound Classifier" sample, which says it can "Detect and identify hundreds of sounds by using a trained classifier." To get the exact labels, query the request at runtime. The page's example does this:

```swift
func makeRequest(_ customModel: MLModel? = nil) throws -> SNClassifySoundRequest {
    // If applicable, create a request with a custom sound classification model.
    if let model = customModel {
        let customRequest = try SNClassifySoundRequest(mlModel: model)
        return customRequest
    }

    // Create a request with the Sound Analysis model.
    let version1 = SNClassifierIdentifier.version1
    let request = try SNClassifySoundRequest(classifierIdentifier: version1)

    return request
}

let classifySoundRequest = try makeRequest()

// Prints every label in the request's sound classification model.
print(classifySoundRequest.knownClassifications)
```

The page describes `knownClassifications` as "A string array that contains every prediction label in the request's underlying sound classifier model."

content.content:
Decode the export mix as float before the gain, then offer 24-bit WAV/AIFF
enhancement,needs-triage,ai-drafted,low-priority,icebox
**The export's write pass reads the mix as 16-bit integers before the loudness gain, so a mix over full scale is measured whole and written clipped.** `ExportWriter.decodedAudioSettings` (`app/Sources/ExporterWriter.swift:873-881`, `AVLinearPCMBitDepthKey: 16` at `:877`, `AVLinearPCMIsFloatKey: false` at `:878`) is the format the mix is read through, and `applyGain` (`:537`) scales `Int16` samples with `LoudnessInt16Gain`. The measurement pass reads the same mix as 32-bit float (`ExporterLoudness.swift:77`), so a normalised export that turns a hot mix DOWN still carries the clipping. Today the difference is reported, not removed: `ExportLoudness.mixClipped` (`Loudness.swift:205`) is what says the figures are the mix's.

Not filed as a bug: the doc comment at `ExporterWriter.swift:860-872` records the trade-off deliberately (a float decode changes the format description every encoder in the file consumes, hence every existing export's bytes), and the clip is surfaced to the user.

24-bit rides on the same change: the same dictionary is what the `lpcm` rows write straight out (`audio_wav`, `audio_aiff`, ProRes), so widening it is where 24-bit comes from. `core/src/export_table.rs:370-375` and spec §7.8 (`designs/spec/07.8-export.md:116-120`) defer it as a request, not a row: an `audio_bits` override beside the bitrates, measured first. A mismatch between the decode and the encoder settings is a file of noise, not an error.

Checked at `976e674`: all cited lines say what is described; no `audio_bits` exists in `core/` or `app/`.

**Done when:** (1) the write pass decodes float (or gains before quantising), a normalised export of a mix peaking over 0 dBFS has no clipped samples, and every other preset's audio is proved byte- or sample-identical to before (or the change is recorded and re-proved); (2) an `audio_bits` export override (16 | 24) lands in the core's export settings, spec §7.8, the export tool and the sheet, and a 24-bit WAV and AIFF each decode to the expected samples (ffmpeg PCM comparison in `tools/proof/`).

Effects E8: offline voice effects
enhancement,spec,ai-drafted,low-priority,icebox
**Deferred by the user on 2026-09-15.** In the user's words: "we'll eventually add color grading and LUT import, but not now". Nothing of it is in the tree.

**E8 adds 16 voice effects (pitch, telephone, radio, reverbs and so on), rendered offline to a cached file rather than live.**

Shape (survey §6 E8, §5a; ADR `designs/adr/effects-survey.md`):
- `audio.voice` is `{kind, amount, pitch −12…12}`, one per clip. There are 16 kinds:
  - voice: pitch, high, deep, robot;
  - tone: bass, treble, bright, telephone, radio;
  - character: lofi, distorted;
  - space: echo, room, hall, plate, cathedral.
- Each kind is a FIXED chain of Apple units: TimePitch, EQ, Distortion, Delay and Reverb. No chain comes from Concat.
- A new `VoiceRenderer.swift` renders the clip's source WINDOW to `cache/voiced/<digest>.caf`. The digest covers stamp, reversed, window, kind, amount, pitch and a chain version. This is a per-clip window cache; the whole-media cache was overturned by measurement.
- `CompositionBuilder` substitutes the file per clip and plays DRY while a render is pending. Tails are cut at the clip end.
- The render contract, every line measured:
  - 48 kHz STEREO, because reverb given mono aborts the process;
  - an `AVAudioPlayerNode`, and schedule → `start()` → `play()`;
  - fixed 4,096-frame calls;
  - presets through `auAudioUnit.currentPreset`, every parameter set and clamped;

Adobe's help pages cover the Essential Sound route and the manual effects route.

- **Essential Sound panel:** In the Repair section, you tick DeHum or DeEss and set a 0–10 slider for each. Select the checkbox for the property you want to reduce, and then use the slider to adjust the level between 0 and 10.
- **DeHum:** It targets a single-frequency hum, at 50 Hz in Europe, Asia, and Africa or 60 Hz in the Americas. Stray power cables routed near audio cables are a typical cause. You can select the hum level depending on the clip.
- **DeEss:** It targets harsh, high-frequency S sounds. Sibilance in vocal recordings that cause s -sounds is created by breathing or air movement between the microphone and the singer's mouth.
- **Manual control:** The Effect Controls route gives more precision. The DeHummer has Frequency, Q, Gain, and harmonic settings, and if you're unsure of the precise frequency, drag this setting back and forth while previewing audio. The DeEsser has a Broadband or Multiband mode, and Multiband is best for most audio content, but slightly increases processing time.
- **Notch Filter alternative:** Use this effect to remove narrow frequency bands, such as a 60-Hz hum, while leaving all surrounding frequencies untouched.

Sources: Adobe's "Repair dialogue in Premiere" page, the Essential Sound panel page, and the audio effects library page. The effects library page is dated older, so check the current UI if the menus differ.

  strip and action lane, and its track is sized as a picture track.

Filmstrips and waveforms come from a cache made for each media file after
import, so they fill in a moment after a file is added.

### The action lane

A clip that has actions (keyframed segments) gets an **action lane** right
under its name strip. Each action is a band. At Medium and Large each band
shows its number in time order (and a zoom glyph for a zoom action); at Large
it also lists the properties it changes; at Small the bands are plain bars.
The selected action is solid, its span is washed down the clip, and it is
shaded on the ruler.

Hover a band to highlight it and show its 5 pt grips at both ends (a band
15 pt wide or less has none). The pointer is an open hand over the body and
a resize arrow over a grip.

Click a band to select the clip and that action; the playhead also moves to
the action's end, so the preview shows its end state. Drag a band's body to
move the action, or drag a grip to resize it. After a move or resize the
action stays selected and the playhead goes to its new end. When exactly one
clip is selected, playing or scrubbing into one of its actions' spans
selects that action. Esc leaves it, and ⌫ removes it.
Everything else about actions is on
[Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

# Audio survey: what professional editors offer, and what Frame Job lacks

- **Status:** Survey, 2026-10-30. Proposals only: nothing here is a spec §11
  decision. A phase that takes one up records it in
  `designs/spec/11-decisions/audio.md` (the AU- series, begun by AU-1) before
  its code.
- **The question (owner, 2026-10-30):** "Review the audio editing features of
  other video editing tools. What other audio editing features should we
  support to be considered a professional-grade tool?"
- **The immediate case:** a quiet but clean RØDE USB desktop-microphone voice
  recording, `samples/Rode-usb-mic.m4a`, which the owner wants to turn into
  usable audio for videos. §2 measures it, and §5 marks which gaps it needs
  first.
- **Method:** every claim about another editor cites the vendor's own manual,
  help page, new-features guide or release notes (§7). Three limits on that:
  - **Adobe:** helpx.adobe.com refused direct fetches (HTTP 403). Premiere
    claims are therefore taken from search-engine excerpts of the cited
    helpx pages, not from a full read.
  - **Blackmagic:** the DaVinci Resolve Reference Manual (thousands of pages)
    was not read. Resolve claims come from Blackmagic's New Features Guides
    for 19, 19.1 and 20, and from its product and What's New pages.
  - **CapCut:** it publishes no help pages for its audio tools that I could
    find. Its claims come from CapCut's own marketing articles and are marked
    *unverified*.

  Apple framework claims were checked against developer.apple.com and the
  macOS 26.2 SDK headers.

## Contents

1. [Frame Job today](#1-frame-job-today)
2. [The owner's recording, measured](#2-the-owners-recording-measured)
3. [What the other editors offer](#3-what-the-other-editors-offer)
4. [Feature matrix](#4-feature-matrix)
5. [The gaps, tiered](#5-the-gaps-tiered)
6. [Sample recordings to add](#6-sample-recordings-to-add)

## Spec §1's non-goals, and the flags below

Spec §1 (`designs/spec/01-what-this-is.md`) lists as a deliberate non-goal
"audio beyond what shipped (volume, fades, duck, pan, compressor, noise
reduction, peak normalize, the transition crossfade and the export's loudness
target — M3 and §11 R5-2; so no EQ, mix buses or Audio Units, while offline
voice effects are deferred rather than out)". The same section sets the bar
"without Final Cut's magnetic timeline, roles, multicam, scopes, or a plugin
ecosystem", and lists "a plugin system" (§11 G-1) as a non-goal.

Every proposal below goes beyond "what shipped", and the owner's audio pass
has already begun lifting that umbrella clause (AU-1 raised the volume
ceiling). Each gap is therefore flagged only against the **named** items:

| Flag | Non-goal it would lift |
|---|---|
| **NG-EQ** | "no EQ" |
| **NG-BUS** | "no … mix buses" |
| **NG-AU** | "no … Audio Units". This survey reads it as *hosting Audio Units as a feature*. Frame Job already runs one of Apple's units internally: `AVAudioUnitTimePitch` renders speed-ramp audio (`app/Sources/RampAudioRenderer+TimePitch.swift`). A gap built on an Apple unit is marked **NG-AU?** for the owner to rule on. |
| **NG-ROLES** | "roles" (the §1 bar) |
| **NG-PLUGIN** | "a plugin system" (§11 G-1) |
| **E8** | "offline voice effects are deferred rather than out" (issue #123) |

### How it is built, as far as it bears on feasibility

- **Per-clip effects run in a tap, before the fader.** Pan, mono,
  compressor and noise reduction run in one `MTAudioProcessingTap` per
  composition audio track, created PreEffects. Volume, fades and ducking
  come after it, as the plan's envelope applied as volume ramps
  (`app/Sources/AudioTap.swift`). A new per-clip stage therefore sees the
  clip at its recorded level, before Volume (up to ×32) is applied.
- **The preview has no post-mix insert; the export does.** Each track carries
  exactly one tap, and the metering build already uses it
  (`AudioTap.swift`). The export reads a 32-bit float mix and applies its
  loudness gain there (`app/Sources/ExporterAudioGain.swift`).
- **Heavy or pitch-changing work renders offline.** Speed-ramp audio is
  rendered offline into the package's `cache/` (`speed.md`). E8's design
  (#123) measured the same pattern for Apple's effect units, because the live
  tap "cannot host a pitch shifter".

## 2. The owner's recording, measured

`samples/Rode-usb-mic.m4a`: 30.4 s, AAC mono, 48 kHz. Measured 2026-10-30
with ffmpeg's `astats` and `ebur128=peak=true` and a numpy pass over
50 ms windows and FFT bands. The script lived in a scratch folder and is not
in the tree.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Sample peak / true peak | −18.6 dBFS / −18.5 dBTP |
| Integrated loudness | −44.7 LUFS |
| Loudness range (LRA) | 21.1 LU (LRA low −64.3 LUFS, high −43.1 LUFS) |
| 50 ms RMS, 10th percentile (the floor) | −64.3 dBFS |
| 50 ms RMS, 90th / 99th percentile (speech) | −43.2 / −35.8 dBFS |
| Windows within 6 dB of the floor | 65 % |
| Pause noise below 80 Hz / below 300 Hz | 20 % / 78 % of its energy |
| Tonal peaks at 50, 100 / 60, 120 Hz in pauses | 9–11 dB over neighbouring bins, in both mains families |
| 5–9 kHz vs 0.3–4 kHz on active windows | median −22.4 dB, 95th percentile −0.2 dB |

What the numbers say:

1. **Peak normalize and the export's loudness target both stop near
   −27 LUFS.** The peak-to-loudness ratio is 26 dB. Normalize to −1 dBFS
   applies +17.6 dB, so the clip lands at about −27.1 LUFS. A −16 LUFS
   target needs +28.7 dB and −14 LUFS needs +30.7 dB, which would put the
   true peak at about +10 or +12 dBTP. The export's gain is capped at the
   −1 dBTP ceiling, so the file lands at the same −27 LUFS, "quieter than
   asked". Reaching either target takes **about 11–13 dB of peak
   reduction**: a compressor and a limiter, not just gain.
2. **At its defaults, the shipped compressor never acts on this file.** Its
   threshold is −18 dB and it runs before Volume, while the file peaks at
   −18.6 dBFS. To use it here, a person has to know to drop the threshold
   to around −40 dB.
3. **The lift raises the floor into earshot.** After +28.7 dB, the pause
   floor sits around −36 dBFS, between sentences that make up 65 % of the
   windows. The pause noise is low: 78 % of it lies below 300 Hz, but only
   20 % below 80 Hz. A high-pass at 80 Hz takes about 1 dB off it. The rest
   shares the voice's own range, so it needs noise reduction, voice
   isolation, or a downward expander that closes in the pauses.
4. **The 21 LU loudness range is the pauses, not the voice.** LRA's low end,
   −64.3 LUFS, *is* the noise floor: its −68.4 LUFS relative gate lets the
   quiet stretches in. A dialogue leveller is not this file's first need.
5. **Mains hum and sibilance are not indicated.** Both are inconclusive.
   The low bins rise by a similar amount in the 50 Hz and 60 Hz families,
   which reads as the low-frequency slope rather than a hum. Fricatives
   reach the voice band's energy in 5 % of active windows, which needs a
   listen. Sibilance matters more once EQ presence and heavy compression
   are added.

Not measured: what the shipped noise reducer does to this file's floor.
That is the first comparison a phase should make, with Apple's
`AUSoundIsolation` as the other side (see A4).

    [S1]. Frame Job: the compressor. All are compressors rather than slow
    gain riders.
13. Premiere: Auto Tag plus per-type Auto-Match [P16, P3].
14. Descript: Studio Sound is one toggle [D1].
15. Driven by the sound: Resolve by the source signal [R3]; Premiere by
    detected dialogue, writing keyframes [P4].
16. Driven by the timeline: Descript by clip presence [D3]; Camtasia by
    clip extent [T1]; ScreenFlow by overlap [S1]; Frame Job by clip extent
    (audio.md).
17. ScreenFlow: audio actions [S1]. Frame Job: volume, mute and fades
    through actions on an action lane, with no line on the waveform.
18. Frame Job: linear fades; the transition crossfade is constant power
    (R5-2).
19. FCP: roles and audio lanes [F8]; no fader mixer was found.
20. Camtasia: a project master gain [T2]. ScreenFlow: a per-clip channel
    mixer [S1]. Frame Job: track mute and solo only.
21. FCP: effects on compound clips [F3].
22. Descript: a linked article, "Export individual sequence tracks as mono
    files", was not read [D4].
23. Descript: mono or stereo output [D4]. Camtasia: Mix to Mono [T2]. Frame
    Job: Mix to mono (averages all channels) and pan. None can pick a single
    channel.
24. Camtasia: Separate Video and Audio [T2]. Frame Job: Detach Audio,
    which is one way.
25. Frame Job: the live meter is peak and RMS. LUFS appears only in the
    export's report.
26. Frame Job: needs a cloud transcript (AssemblyAI, the person's own key).
27. Descript: Reverb, Distortion, Bitcrusher, Flanger [D2]. Camtasia: Pitch,
    Mac only [T1]. ScreenFlow: delay [S1].

**Reading the matrix:** Frame Job's clip strip (volume, fades, noise
reduction, compressor, pan, mono) and its clean-up tools already match the
creator tier: Camtasia, ScreenFlow and much of Descript. Against the three
professional editors, the shortfall falls into four groups:

- **Dynamics:** limiting, gating or expansion, and loudness-target
  normalization.
- **Tone:** EQ, de-essing and hum notches.
- **ML voice clean-up.**
- **Mix structure:** track faders, buses, animating any parameter, and
  stems.

## 5. The gaps, tiered

Each gap gives what it is, who has it, why it matters here, a one-line
feasibility note on Apple Silicon and macOS 26 (AVFoundation, no ffmpeg),
and any non-goal flag. **Mic** marks what `samples/Rode-usb-mic.m4a` needs,
per §2's measurements.

### What the quiet desktop-mic recording needs first

The order below follows the §2 measurements, not assumptions:

| Order | Gap | Why, from §2 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A1 limiter and A2 loudness-target normalize, together | Peak normalize and the gain-only export target both stop near −27 LUFS; −16 or −14 LUFS needs 11–13 dB of peak reduction |
| 2 | B1 a voice preset chain | The compressor exists but is inert at its defaults on a −18.6 dBFS peak, because it runs before Volume |
| 3 | A5 expander, or A4 voice isolation, beside the shipped noise reduction | After the lift, the pause floor sits around −36 dBFS in 65 % of the windows |
| 4 | A3 high-pass and EQ | A standard step, though only about 1 dB here; presence and tone after that |
| Later | A6 de-esser, B3 leveller, A7 hum removal | Not indicated by the measurements: sibilance inconclusive, LRA is the pauses, no clear hum |

### Tier A: needed to be called professional-grade

**A1. A true-peak limiter, and an export loudness target that reaches its
number.** **Mic: first.**

- **What:** a lookahead, true-peak limiter on the clip strip and on the
  export's mix. The export's loudness stage limits instead of capping gain,
  so −14 LUFS means −14 LUFS.
- **Who:**
  - Resolve: the channel-strip limiter [R1], and Deliver's "Optimize
    loudness and peak" [R3].
  - FCP: Limiter and Adaptive Limiter [F4].
  - Premiere: Hard Limiter [P8], and Media Encoder's true-peak limiter
    inside loudness normalization [P10].
  - Descript: Limiter [D2].
  - ScreenFlow: peak limiting [S1].
- **Why:** quiet voice recordings have a high peak-to-loudness ratio (26 dB
  here), so gain alone hits the ceiling long before any streaming target.
- **Feasibility:** `AUPeakLimiter` exists (attack, decay, pre-gain
  −40…+40 dB) [A3], but true-peak detection is not documented for it. A
  limiter written beside `AudioDSP.swift`'s compressor, oversampled, is the
  surer route. The mix stage belongs where the export already gains in
  float (`ExporterAudioGain.swift`). A clip limiter in the tap must carry
  the clip's gain itself, because Volume is applied after the tap. The
  preview has no post-mix insert, so a preview master limiter is an open
  design question.
- **Flags:** none named (it is dynamics, like the shipped compressor).
  **NG-AU?** if built on `AUPeakLimiter`.

**A2. Loudness-target clip normalization and level matching.** **Mic:
first.**

- **What:** "Normalize to −16 LUFS" per clip, measured over the played
  range with the BS.1770 gate, and optionally speech-only. Also "match these
  clips' loudness". A clip's measured LUFS is shown in the inspector.
- **Who:** Premiere Auto-Match, with the clip's LUFS displayed [P3]; Resolve
  clip normalization [R1] and the AI Level Matcher [R2]; Descript's LUFS
  export options [D4].
- **Why:** peak normalize lands this file at −27 LUFS while a louder take
  lands elsewhere. Loudness is what a viewer hears, and clips cut together
  need to match.
- **Feasibility:** the BS.1770-4 measurement already exists for the export
  (`Loudness.swift`, `ExporterLoudness.swift`). It needs only a per-clip
  read like Normalize's. The ×32 ceiling (AU-1) covers the gain, and A1
  catches the peaks.
- **Flags:** none named.

**A3. EQ: high-pass, low-pass, shelves and parametric bands, with voice
presets.** **Mic: fourth.**

- **Who:** every professional editor and two creator tools:
  - Resolve: a 6-band clip EQ and a track EQ with 24 dB/octave filters [R1,
    R2, R3].
  - FCP: Equalization presets, Channel EQ and Match [F1, F2, F4].
  - Premiere: Parametric Equalizer and Clarity EQ [P6, P8].
  - Descript: EQs and high-pass [D2].
  - ScreenFlow: EQ [S1].
- **Why:** desk mics pick up rumble, desk thumps and plosives, and EQ is
  the basic tone control. Several other gaps are built from it (A6, A7,
  B6).
- **Feasibility:** `AVAudioUnitEQ` offers parametric, low-pass, high-pass,
  shelf and band-stop types [A7], and `AUNBandEQ` the same per band [A6].
  Biquads in the tap are cheap DSP of Frame Job's own and stay live.
- **Flags:** **NG-EQ**.

**A4. ML voice isolation (speech enhancement).** **Mic: third (with A5).**

- **Who:** FCP Voice Isolation [F1]; Resolve Voice Isolation (Studio) [R2,
  R6]; Premiere Enhance Speech [P1]; Descript Studio Sound (cloud) [D1];
  Camtasia AI Noise Removal [T3]; CapCut Enhance voice (*unverified*) [C2].
- **Why:** this is now the baseline one-control fix for noisy rooms and
  cheap microphones, and the creator audience expects it. Frame Job's
  reducer handles only steady noise.
- **Feasibility:** Apple's `AUSoundIsolation` runs on the device (macOS
  13+). Its parameters are a wet/dry mix and a sound type; the
  HighQualityVoice model needs macOS 15+ [A1]. Render it offline into
  `cache/`, as speed-ramp audio is, with a wet/dry Amount. Its latency, CPU
  cost and quality on this file are unmeasured.
- **Flags:** **NG-AU?**

**A5. Downward expander or noise gate.** **Mic: third.**

- **Who:** Resolve's expander/gate on every strip [R1]; FCP Expander,
  Noise Gate and Spectral Gate [F4].
- **Why:** gain lifts the floor (to around −36 dBFS here). An expander
  pulls the pauses down without touching the speech, and it handles
  non-steady room noise that a spectral reducer can't learn.
- **Feasibility:** `AUDynamicsProcessor` has an expansion ratio and
  threshold [A4]. A stage written beside the compressor reuses its
  envelope follower.
- **Flags:** none named. **NG-AU?** if built on `AUDynamicsProcessor`.

**A6. De-esser.**

- **Who:** Resolve [R1]; FCP DeEsser 2 [F4]; Premiere DeEss and DeEsser
  [P5].
- **Why:** EQ presence and heavy compression, both needed for quiet voices,
  bring sibilance forward. For this file it is inconclusive (§2).
- **Feasibility:** no Apple de-esser unit was found. Either a
  side-chain-filtered compressor in `AudioDSP`, or `AUMultiBandCompressor`
  (four bands) [A5].
- **Flags:** **NG-EQ** (a de-esser is a dynamic EQ).

**A7. Hum removal: a notch at 50 or 60 Hz and its harmonics.**

- **Who:** FCP Hum Removal [F1]; Premiere DeHum, DeHummer and Notch Filter
  [P5, P8]; Resolve de-hummer [R1].
- **Why:** ground-loop hum from USB and laptop chargers is common in
  desktop setups. A notch removes it surgically where a spectral reducer
  smears. Not indicated for this file (§2).
- **Feasibility:** band-stop filters at f0 and its multiples:
  `AVAudioUnitEQ`'s band-stop type [A7], or biquads in the tap.
- **Flags:** **NG-EQ**.

**A8. Live loudness metering, and a per-clip loudness readout.**

- **Who:** Resolve loudness meters and graph [R1]; FCP MultiMeter (LUFS,
  true peak) [F5]; Premiere Loudness Meter [P9].
- **Why:** mixing to a target needs momentary, short-term and integrated
  LUFS and true peak while playing, not only after export.
- **Feasibility:** K-weighting and gating already exist (`Loudness.swift`).
  The metering build already reads every track's tap and applies the plan's
  envelope (`AudioTap.swift`, `LevelMeter.swift`).
- **Flags:** none.

**A9. Animate every audio parameter, and draw volume on the clip.**

- **What:** pan, EQ and effect parameters over time, plus a rubber-band
  volume line on the waveform.
- **Who:** Resolve automation of "virtually any control" [R1]; FCP's Audio
  Animation editor [F11]; Premiere clip and track keyframes with the Pen
  tool, and automation modes [P11, P12]; Camtasia audio points [T2].
- **Why:** a static pan or EQ per clip is a creator-tier limit. Professional
  mixes ride levels inside clips, and Frame Job's actions can't reach pan
  or effects today (audio.md).
- **Feasibility:** core and UI work with no new framework. The tap already
  schedules settings by clip span (`AudioDSPSpan`); per-parameter envelopes
  would extend that schedule.
- **Flags:** none.

**A10. Split edits (J- and L-cuts) that keep sync, and reversible
detaching.**

- **Who:** FCP Expand Audio and split edits [F10]; Premiere Unlink and
  ⌥-drag [P17].
- **Why:** J- and L-cuts are the most common dialogue edit. Frame Job's
  Detach Audio is one way, and "no control … switches a clip's audio back
  on" (audio.md).
- **Feasibility:** a model and timeline-gesture change; no framework
  needed.
- **Flags:** none.

**A11. Stems: each track, or each group of tracks, as its own file.**

- **Who:** FCP roles as separate files or a multitrack QuickTime [F9];
  Descript per-track mono files (an article title only) [D4]. Resolve and
  Premiere were not verified.
- **Why:** hand-off to a mixer, music-and-effects versions, a
  voice-without-music version for translation.
- **Feasibility:** per-track files can reuse the export with the other
  tracks silenced. A multitrack MOV would need several `AVAssetWriterInput`s
  (unverified here).
- **Flags:** **NG-ROLES** only if it is done by role rather than by track.

**A12. Track faders and track or bus processing.**

- **Who:** Resolve's mixer, buses and FlexBus [R1]; Premiere's Audio Track
  Mixer and submixes [P11]. FCP gets by without a mixer, through roles and
  compound clips [F3, F8].
- **Why:** "music 6 dB down everywhere" is one fader, not forty clip edits.
  A compressor or limiter across a whole voice track behaves differently
  from per-clip ones at clip boundaries.
- **Feasibility:** a track fader is an envelope in the plan. Track effects
  have no natural home, because composition audio tracks are not timeline
  tracks (`AudioTap.swift` notes the A/B assignment). They need a design
  spike.
- **Flags:** **NG-BUS**.

**A13. 24-bit (and float-decoded) audio export.**

- **Who:** not verified across editors.
- **Why:** a delivery and archival expectation.
- **Feasibility:** issue #86 has the design: a float decode before the gain,
  then an `audio_bits` override.
- **Flags:** none.

### Tier B: expected by the creator and screencast audience

**B1. A one-click "Enhance voice" chain.** **Mic: second.**

- **What:** high-pass → noise reduction or isolation → compressor set
  relative to the clip's measured level → limiter → loudness target. It
  writes ordinary clip settings that a person can then edit.
- **Who:** FCP Enhance Audio [F1]; Resolve AI Audio Assistant (Studio)
  [R2]; Premiere Auto Tag plus Auto-Match [P16, P3]; Descript Studio Sound
  [D1].
- **Why:** a screencaster wants one button. The shipped compressor proves
  that defaults fixed in dBFS fail on a quiet mic (§2).
- **Feasibility:** no DSP beyond A1–A5. The assistant and agents get it
  through the same tool (agent parity).
- **Flags:** inherits its parts' flags.

**B2. Speech-aware ducking.**

- **What:** keyed by voice activity, not clip extent, with a pre-roll. It
  is drawn as an envelope the person can see and edit.
- **Who:** Premiere Auto Ducking, which writes keyframes [P4]; Resolve's
  signal-keyed Ducker with lookahead [R3, R4].
- **Why:** today's ducking holds music down through every pause of a long
  voice clip (audio.md).
- **Feasibility:** the on-device voice model already runs per media for
  Remove Silences (`cleanup-tools.md`). Its speech spans can shape the duck
  envelope in the plan, deterministically, with no new framework.
- **Flags:** none.

**B3. Dialogue leveller (a slow gain rider).**

- **Who:** Resolve Dialogue Leveler [R2, R3].
- **Why:** a speaker who leans in and out, or a two-person recording. Not
  indicated for this file, whose LRA is the pauses (§2).
- **Feasibility:** computed offline from short-term loudness into the
  envelope, or a slow stage of Frame Job's own.
- **Flags:** none.

**B4. De-reverb.**

- **Who:** Premiere Reduce Reverb and DeReverb [P5, P8]; Descript Studio
  Sound "echo" [D1]; Resolve's Dialogue Separator ambience [R3].
- **Why:** laptop microphones in untreated rooms.
- **Feasibility:** no Apple de-reverb unit was found. Whether
  `AUSoundIsolation` removes reverberation is unverified.
- **Flags:** **NG-AU?** if it rides on A4.

**B5. Audio scrubbing.**

- **Who:** FCP audio skimming [F14].
- **Why:** finding a word by ear while dragging the playhead. Frame Job's
  scrub is silent (`timeline.md`).
- **Feasibility:** unverified. It needs short-grain playback at the scrub
  position.
- **Flags:** none.

**B6. Match one clip to another: EQ, level and room.**

- **Who:** FCP Match Audio [F2]; Resolve AI EQ Matcher, Level Matcher and
  Dialogue Matcher [R2].
- **Why:** a camera's scratch audio cut against the RØDE, or two sessions
  on different days.
- **Feasibility:** a spectrum difference becomes an EQ curve (needs A3). The
  level half is A2.
- **Flags:** **NG-EQ**.

**B7. Channel selection: left only, right only, dual mono.**

- **Who:** FCP channel configuration [F7]; Premiere Modify ▸ Audio Channels
  [P13]; Resolve channel mapping [R1, R4]; ScreenFlow per-channel pan and
  level [S1].
- **Why:** USB and XLR interfaces often record a mono mic onto one channel
  of a stereo file. Frame Job's Mix to mono averages the channels, which
  lands 6 dB down when one channel is silent.
- **Feasibility:** a channel pick before the mono fold in the tap. Trivial
  DSP, plus a model field.
- **Flags:** none.

**B8. Clean-up at record time.**

- **Who:** Resolve's Voiceover tool, with Voice Isolation, Dialog Leveler
  and Stereo Fixer while recording [R2]; Descript Studio Sound while
  recording [D1].
- **Why:** a voice-over should land ready to use.
- **Feasibility:** the raw file is kept, and the B1 chain is applied as
  clip settings when the Microphone clip lands, so no new DSP. Apple's
  voice processing on the input node [A13] is call-style echo cancellation
  and is not proposed.
- **Flags:** none.

**B9. Fade and crossfade curve shapes.**

- **Who:** FCP Linear, S-curve, +3 dB and −3 dB [F13]; Premiere Constant
  Gain, Constant Power and Exponential [P19].
- **Feasibility:** envelope shapes in the core's plan.
- **Flags:** none.

**B10. Voice effects (E8).**

- **Who:** FCP Pitch Shifter, Vocal Transformer and reverbs [F4]; Resolve
  Voice Convert (Studio) [R2]; Camtasia Pitch (Mac) [T1]; Descript's
  creative effects [D2]; CapCut voice changer (*unverified*) [C1].
- **Feasibility:** already designed and measured as E8 (#123): fixed chains
  of Apple units rendered offline.
- **Flags:** **E8**; **NG-AU?**
